The calculated risks are often considered notional rather than true actuarial or statistical values. The calculated risks include, for example, the potential failures that can be modeled by normal design rules and formulas, but not the failures due to human error, blunders, or a very limited technological understanding of the structure's true behavior. Nevertheless, as notional measures of risk, the values obtained from a consistent reliability model serve as valuable guides for decisions that must be made. Confidence in the reliability-based design process is gained by calibrating to existing design practice and experience.

COMM. LRFD.2.0 THE LRFD FORMAT

Research projects sponsored by API reviewed the RP2A "Recommended Practice for Planning, Designing and Constructing Fixed Offshore Platforms" and concluded that the current implicit approach to safety does not provide structures with consistent component reliability. The API therefore decided to modify its current method of checking component safety, known as a working stress design (WSD) format, to a multiple safety factor format known as load and resistance factor design (LRFD). In WSD, a component is checked with an equation of the form:

$$\frac{\text{N o m i a l S t r e n g t h}}{\text{S a f e t y F a c t o r}} \geq \text{S u m o f N o m i a l L o a d s}$$

Only one safety factor is used and the safety margin and hence the reliability will depend on the range of design application. In the LRFD approach, partial safety factors are used in the format:

Resistance Factor x Nominal Strength >

Load Effect due to the Sum of Factored External Loads

where nominal strengths and loads may be the same as WSD, but each term is multiplied by its respective load or resistance factor. The load and resistance factors are each matched during the code formulation to their respective uncertainties thereby reducing reliability variations over the anticipated range of applications. These factors must be calibrated by code committees using a reliability model and design experience and then tabulated for routine design practice.

An LRFD type format has been adopted by several structural codes in the United States such as ACI (reinforced concrete) and AASHTO (bridges). LRFD is being promoted by the National Bureau of Standards for building design, and an LRFD code has been issued by AISC for steel structures. This directly impacts offshore design since API RP2A excerpts major portions of the AISC code, especially for checking platform deck components. The AISC-LRFD code cannot be easily adapted to the API WSD provisions.

Comm. LRFD.2.1 Basic Terminology. The LRFD checking equations will appear herein with the following basic notation. A component meets the criterion if:

$$\phi \mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{n}} \geq \mathrm{Q} \quad \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \tag{Comm.LRFD-1}$$

where:

$$\begin{array}{l} \phi = \text{c o m p o n e n t} \\ \mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{n}} = \text{n o m i n a l} \\ Q = \text{f a c t o r e d} \\ Q = \Sigma \gamma_{i} F_{i}. \tag{Comm.LRFD-2} \\ \end{array}$$

where:

$$\begin{array}{l} \gamma_{i} = \text{l o a d f a c t o r f o r l o a d t y p e i}, \\ \begin{array}{l} \mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{i}} \\ = \text{n o m i n a l} \end{array} \\ \end{array}$$

This simple notation will be expanded for cases of strength interaction ratios in which separate resistance factors may appear with each strength term. Furthermore, load factors are applied to the nominal loadings before the structural analyses are performed to calculate member forces. The load combination shown is for illustration of the concept and not the actual arithmetic combination of member forces. Factoring the load before doing the analysis is necessary whenever nonlinear foundation support is being modeled.

COMM. LRFD.3.0 RP2A-LRFD DEVELOPMENT

The reliability model adopted for establishing the load and resistance factors is based on the safety index beta （$\beta)$ method in which uncertainties are described by means and coefficients of variation (standard deviation divided by the mean). It leads to a reliability expression of the form:

$$\text{S a f e t y I n d e x ,} \beta = \frac{\text{M e a n S a f e t y M a r g i n}}{\text{U n c e r t a i n t y L e v e l}}$$

The safety index is a measure of reliability and is related to the number of standard deviations that the mean safety margin falls in the safe region, e.g., when resistance is greater than the load.

The safety index has two important features for developing structural codes:

1. The safety index does not require explicit risk values. It is, however, a valid measure of risk without the legal, social, economic and psychological impact of risks expressed as probabilities of failure.   
2. Designers do not need to learn probability theory. The reliability analysis becomes transparent to the designer, since $\beta$ is only used by code writers in deriving the design factors which are then used independently of the reliability theory.

Past experience combined with measured data are used to calibrate the load and resistance factors to produce designs that will have, on the average, reliabilities similar to that of existing designs produced by WSD. LRFD produces designs with more uniform $\beta$ than current WSD even when the average values are similar, thereby improving overall reliability.

In the RP2A-LRFD there are no preassigned $\beta$ levels. Rather, a data base was compiled for a range of typical platform components such as piles, jacket braces, horizontals, etc., for a variety of water depths, geometries, grouted and ungrouted cases. These examples from existing platforms provided a direct comparison of LRFD with present practice.

A statistical data base on uncertainties of loads and component strengths was assembled and is presented in the respective commentary sections. It is based on experimental distributions as well as variations due to intended simplifications in design equations (both the so-called natural and subjective variabilities).

Utilizing a full range of platform types, a set of safety indices was computed based on sizes derived from current WSD rules. The calculation of $\beta$ was done with structural reliability techniques which are now well known and described in both API PRAC 22 reports, References COMM1-9, and other publications. The calibration procedure then established target safety indices upon which to determine partial safety factors in the LRFD format. In this way LRFD designs may have the same average safety （$\beta)$ as current WSD designs but will be more uniform and have less fluctuation about the target $\beta$ . As an illustration, in current design practice, platforms with high gravity load (compared with environmental load) generally have higher $\beta$ 's (more reliability) because of low uncertainty in gravity loads. This influence is balanced by LRFD with smaller gravity load factors compared with environmental load factors.

The entire reliability-based RP2A-LRFD checking format was tested for practicality by checking several platform designs for shallow, moderate and deep water. The platform design checks are described in this Commentary by reference to Platforms A, B, C, etc. Further details of these platforms appear in the API reports. This checking was carried out by several different design firms who incorporated the LRFD provisions in their analysis procedures. They checked feasibility in both computer-based checks of the jacket, piling, deck and main structural members and also the hand-calculated checks of platform details. These studies also highlighted any significant member sizing differences that arose between WSD and LRFD design. It was demonstrated that LRFD will not result in a significant change in total structure weight, but there will be redistribution of material from gravity designed members to environmentally loaded members.

During the period of LRFD platform design development studies, additional research findings enhanced the statistical data and were incorporated in the partial factors.

Comm. LRFD.3.1 References on RP2A-LRFD Development. The concepts described above were incorporated into this document after several years of research, design comparisons, and industry review. Research began in several industry projects followed by support from the API. The details of this investigation

and development are contained in several references and the API-PRAC-22 documents cited below, References COMM1-11.

The PRAC 79-22 report initiated this work and, based on an industry-wide questionnaire, a plan was developed to achieve a balanced reliability-based design format. The PRAC 80-22 report contains an industry-wide survey of element components and the initial trial format for checking platform components. An initial case of platform checking was performed by PetroMarine Engineers (PME) on Platform A and is reported in PRAC 81-22. A further implementation of the advanced level II checking format for calculating safety indices is also contained in that report. Two more platform checks, done by PME on a shallow water structure (Platform B) and by Brown & Root Inc. on a moderate water depth structure (Platform C), are contained in PRAC 82-22. Various component descriptions and load combination comparisons are also contained in that report. The LRFD applications to deepwater and earthquake design are addressed in PRAC 83-22. Earl & Wright Inc. developed some response values for Platform D out of which the load factor for inertial wave response was produced. Similarly, Brown & Root Inc. addressed earthquakes in a calibration study using Platform E. These projects completed the range of studies needed for bringing out a fully tested and calibrated RP2A-LRFD document. Further reviews, discussions, and summaries are contained in PRAC 85-22 (there is no PRAC 84-22 document). Provisions were revised and recalibrated in the PRAC 86-22 and PRAC 87-22 projects. A tutorial was developed in the PRAC 88-22 project to assist the designer in understanding the background and basis for many of the recommended practices.

In addition to the references cited above that are directly related to the development of the RP2A-LRFD, there have been many publications that have addressed platform reliability; a partial list is given in References COMM12-19.

COMM. LRFD.4.0 THE BETA CALIBRATION PROCESS

The safety index, $\beta$ , is the measure of reliability used to calibrate the new provisions against existing WSD practice. A larger $\beta$ represents a safer situation. Several different beta models are available. The numerical values of $\beta$ depend on the beta model used, i.e., the probability distribution of the random variables and the method for computing $\beta$ . These models include (a) assumed normal or lognormal variables, (b) fitted probability distributions, and (c) exact simulation. A more elaborate beta model offers a more precise relationship between the safety index and an actuarial risk. Simplified models, such as those based on normal or lognormal distributions, are easier to manipulate to derive partial safety factors.

Sensitivity studies performed for the RP2A-LRFD development showed that the choice of beta model did

not significantly affect the partial factors, provided the same model was also used in the calibration process. A major assumption is that past practices and experience should be the guide for the desired safety. The LRFD factors smooth out variations in reliability that may exist in current WSD provisions. These variations existed due to inherent limitations in a single safety factor in WSD and because the offshore platform structural standards were derived from land-based practices for steel buildings made of I-shaped sections.

In the LRFD development, target betas were established after calculating a range of betas for existing platform components designed to RP2A. To avoid large changes in member sizes, the target values for each component type (bending, pile, T joint, etc.) were studied independently. Because all components must use common load factors, some compromises were necessary.

The target betas were obtained after reviewing components from more than fifteen platforms of various water depths and structural geometries, Reference COMM2. Recent research on nominal strength was incorporated where it was felt that it had reached the stage where it would also be appropriate for inclusion in RP2A-WSD.

The first step in beta calibration is to establish the limit state equation. The simplest form which is often applicable is

$$\mathbf{g} \quad = \mathbf{R} - \mathbf{S} = \mathbf{R} - (\mathbf{D} + \mathbf{L} + \mathbf{W} \dots) \dots (\text{C o m m . L R F D - 3})$$

where $\mathbf{g}$ is the safety margin such that if $\mathbf{g}$ is positive the component is safe; $\mathbf{R}$ is the component strength; and D, L, W, etc. are the load effects. In some cases, such as beam-columns, $\mathbf{g}$ cannot be represented as a linear equation. A computer program similar to the NBS advanced first order, second moment (Level II) program (Reference COMM19) was used to calculate beta from the parameters of the random variables in the $\mathbf{g}$ equation.

The second step in calibration is to identify the statistical parameters for each random variable. For component strength, it is important to include all uncertainties including test scatter, material variability, and an estimate of the calculation errors. A common representation for this approach is

$$\mathbf{R} = \mathbf{R}_{\mathrm{n}} \mathbf{M F P}. \tag{Comm.LRFD-4}$$

where:

$\mathbf{R}_{\mathbf{n}}$ = nominal resistance (from a deterministic formula; not a random variable)

$\mathbf{M}$ = material variability

$\mathbf{F}$ = fabrication variability

$\mathbf{P}$ = professional or formula variability

Each of the types of random variables (M, F, P) must be described by their bias (B), the ratio of true mean

divided by nominal value, and uncertainty. The coefficient of variation (V), or ratio of standard deviation divided by mean, was used to represent uncertainty.

The statistical parameters of resistance R may then be approximated by

$$\bar{\mathbf{R}} = \mathbf{R}_{\mathrm{m}} \mathbf{B}_{\mathbf{M}} \mathbf{B}_{\mathbf{F}} \mathbf{B}_{\mathbf{P}} \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \tag{Comm.LRFD-5}$$

where:

$$\bar{\mathbf{R}} = \text{m e a n}$$

$\mathbf{B}_{\mathbf{M}}, \mathbf{B}_{\mathbf{F}}, \mathbf{B}_{\mathbf{p}} =$ bias of material, fabrication, and formula, respectively;

and the coefficient of variation, $\mathbf{V}_{\mathbb{R}}$ , is equal to

$$\mathbf{V}_{\mathbf{R}} = \left(\mathbf{V}_{\mathbf{M}}^{2} + \mathbf{V}_{\mathbf{F}}^{2} + \mathbf{V}_{\mathbf{P}}^{2}\right)^{1 / 2} \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \tag{Comm.LRFD-6}$$

where:

$$\mathbf{V}_{\mathbf{M}}, \mathbf{V}_{\mathbf{F}}, \mathbf{V}_{\mathbf{P}} = \text{c o e f f i c i e n t o f v a r i a t i o n (C O V) o f m a t e r i a l , f a b r i c a t i o n , a n d f o r m u l a , r e s p e c t i v e l y .}$$

The mean and COV of $\mathbf{R}$ are the parameters for the strength variable entering the beta calculation. The nominal resistance, $\mathbf{R}_{\mathbf{n}}$ is first found from the LRFD design checking equation as:

$$\phi \mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{n}} \geq \mathrm{Q}. \tag{Comm.LRFD-7}$$

where $\phi$ is the resistance factor and $\mathbf{Q}$ is the sum of the factored load effects on the component. Substitution gives the mean strength as:

$$\bar{\mathbf{R}} = \mathbf{B}_{\mathbf{R}} \mathbf{R}_{\mathbf{n}} = \frac{\mathbf{B}_{\mathbf{R}}}{\phi} \mathbf{Q} \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \tag{Comm.LRFD-8}$$

The mean resistance is then affected simultaneously by the resistance factor, $\phi$ , (usually less than 1.0) and the resistance bias, $B_{R}$ (depending on the definition of the nominal strength formula). Hence, beta, which depends on the mean resistance, is equally affected by changes in resistance factor and changes in the nominal checking equation. The latter is affected by the fit of the strength equation to the data or analyses (e.g., mean, lowerbound, 95th, percentile, etc.). The reliability model must incorporate any bias in the strength formula in computing beta.

A similar formulation of mean and uncertainty is appropriate for load terms in which random variables include load intensity and analysis uncertainty. Let S be the effect of any load type, then

$$\mathbf{S} = \mathbf{S}_{\mathrm{n}} \mathbf{I} \mathbf{A}. \tag{Comm.LRFD-9}$$

where:

$$\mathbf{S}_{\mathbf{n}} = \text{n o m i n a l l o a d e f f e c t}$$

I = intensity random variable

A $=$ analysis random variable

The load statistics are then

$$\overline{{\mathbf{S}}} = \mathbf{S}_{\mathbf{n}} \overline{{\mathbf{I}}} \overline{{\mathbf{A}}} \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \tag{Comm. LRFD-10}$$

where $\overline{\mathbf{S}}$ is the mean effect of the load type and the coefficient of variation, $\mathbf{V}_{\mathbf{S}}$ , is given by

$$\mathbf{V}_{\mathbf{S}} = \left(\mathbf{V}_{\mathbf{I}}^{2} + \mathbf{V}_{\mathbf{A}}^{2}\right)^{1 / 2}. \tag{Comm.LRFD-11}$$

As with the strength term, the mean load is affected by the definition of the nominal load value, e.g., 100-year period. This load bias must be selected in conjunction with choosing the load factor, $\gamma$ , since each term affects the mean resistance as follows. Substituting for Q gives for a single loading S:

$$\overline{{R}} = \frac{B_{R}}{\phi} Q = \frac{B_{R}}{\phi} \gamma S_{n} = \frac{B_{R}}{\phi} \gamma \frac{\overline{{S}}}{B_{s}} (C o m m. L R F D - 12)$$

where $\mathbf{B}_{\mathbf{S}}$ is the bias for load S.

Beta depends both on natural or inherent variability and also on subjective variability associated with the formulas and models used to calculate loads and strengths. A set of reference uncertainty values was used to calibrate beta and find the partial factors （$\phi$ and $\gamma)$ prescribed herein. In addition, a sensitivity study concluded that within a relatively large variation in the statistical parameters, the prescribed factors still approach the goal of uniform betas, References COMM3,6.

A consequence of subjective uncertainty, however, is that designers who consistently use, for example, more conservative models for nominal load and strength estimation will produce components with higher betas than obtained by more typical designer assumptions. Nevertheless, it is expected that all users of the RP2ALRFD will benefit from having more uniform and consistent betas than would be obtained with existing RP2A-WSD values.

In the absence of adequate statistical data on performance (e.g., earthquakes or piles) the LRFD factors were derived to produce strength levels similar to existing practices. This is referred to as "brute force" calibration.

Component types which had both a data base and performance record were included in the calibration study. The data used are discussed in the Commentary for each checking formula. Depending on the degree of confidence in the data, some target beta values based on past average betas were raised or lowered to approach target values for other component types. However, such target averaging was limited, and no single beta was sought for all platform components. Modifications to LRFD factors in the future may achieve further changes in this direction. Such changes may include economic and system considerations in addition to component reliability.

COMM. LRFD.5.0 SUMMARY OF LRFD IMPACTS ON DESIGN

The current working stress design (WSD) format in RP2A has produced platform structures with high historic reliability levels. The API research studies have

shown, however, that there is considerable scatter implied in the component reliabilities and that a load and resistance factor (LRFD) method would provide greater uniformity. Improved economy can also result especially for platforms with high gravity loads compared to environmental loads. The reliability format can also systematically incorporate new research data and aid in formulating design rules in frontier areas consistent with present practices. One example is the load factor developed for deepwater fixed platform inertial loads. Overall, a reliability format should provide designers with a better understanding of the design process and its role in assuring safety.

It was expected that many organizations would want to compare the existing RP2A with the LRFD checking equations. Such comparisons were made on Platforms A - F. The checking differences were not major and could be explained in terms of positive changes desired with the LRFD format. These included checks on the structures at a 1.35 load factor. Due to possible nonlinear foundation behavior, this factor provides load distributions within the platform at a higher response level corresponding to an overloaded condition.

To the extent possible, the existing form of nominal strength checking equations was maintained for LRFD. That is, only the safety factors are changed. Because of new performance research, however, which occurred while these LRFD provisions were being developed, some new nominal checking equations are introduced which are different from current RP2A but are in anticipation of a likely change to RP2A-WSD in most cases. These are discussed in the appropriate Commentary sections.

Several general conclusions have been observed in these comparisons of LRFD and WSD:

(a) The largest component strength differences between LRFD and WSD should be in the range of $\pm 20\%$ for components which are loaded near their maximum permitted value. In some instances this range may be exceeded. For example, (i) for components with individual load effects of different signs, (ii) when the effect of nonlinear foundation is large, (iii) when there is a change in nominal checking equations from WSD to LRFD, and (iv) when components are not loaded to their maximum permitted level. The effect of nonlinear interaction equation, e.g., cos form, may magnify the differences in utilization ratio between WSD and LRFD.   
(b) LRFD will be more conservative than WSD for environmental load and less conservative for gravity loads. This reflects the greater uncertainty that is present in environmental loads.   
(c) The column stability failure mode will be more conservative for LRFD and the bending strength failure mode will be less conservative. This outcome reflects recent test data for tubular sections. Less reliance is placed on provisions based on rolled section data for column stability and bending. The WSD provisions have been modified to reduce this difference.

(d) LRFD will be more conservative in situations such as overturning when gravity loads oppose environmental loads. This is another example where LRFD methods produce more uniformly safe designs.   
In the course of the platform checks cited above, a number of firms implemented the new checking formulas in their computer design programs. Various surveys indicated that the changes could be implemented with 200-700 man-hours of engineering and programming. Furthermore, the implementation efforts for LRFD were not more severe than some of the recent changes introduced in RP2A.

COMM.LRFD.6.0 GLOSSARY

BETA: See Safety Index below.

BIAS: A ratio of the mean value of a random variable, such as resistance, to the nominal value used in a particular engineering design procedure.

CALIBRATION: A process of adjusting the parameters of a new code, i.e., load and resistance factors as well as nominal design formulas, to achieve reliability safety index values. Calibration is typically done on a range of structures and components obtained by reference to an existing code or taken from actual design experience. The calibration process is introduced to ensure that average reliability of designs to a new code does not intentionally differ from existing codes, and that any variation in reliability of new designs is rationally related to economics or failure consequences.

COEFFICIENT OF VARIATION: A nondimensional measure of uncertainty (variability) of a random variable defined as the ratio of the standard deviation divided by the mean value of a random variable.

LOAD AND RESISTANCE FACTORS DESIGN (LRFD): A design check whereby separate load and resistance factors are applied to nominal loads and nominal resistances.

MEAN: A number which indicates the central tendency of a random variable and which is obtained by summing over all possible values of the random variable the product of the value of the variable and its probability of occurrence. The mean is the average of this sum.

MEDIAN: The value of the random variable defined as the 50th percentile so half of the observations will be less and half greater.

NOMINAL LOAD: The load magnitude used in the design calculation. It may be based on reference to a probability level (e.g., 100-year return period) but not always, such as for rated floor load.

NOMINAL RESISTANCE: The strength equation or magnitude used in the design checking. It may be

based on reference to a probability level, e.g., 95th percentile or be a lower bound on all tests.

PROBABILITY: A measure of the chance that an event will occur expressed on a scale of 0 to 1.

PROBABILITY DISTRIBUTION: A mathematical function describing the probability values corresponding to the outcome of a random variable. Examples include normal, log normal, and Weibull distributions.

PROBABILITY OF FAILURE: In the present context, failure probability refers to the notional, (or calculated), probability of component failure for comparative purposes. It is the calculated probability that the resistance of a component is less than the imposed load effect. It is a comparative or relative measure only and differs from the true or actuarial statistics of failure which include unspecified design and construction factors, system parameters, and the risks of gross error or accident.

RANDOM VARIABLE: A variable associated with random or unpredictable events including natural and subjective (judgment) uncertainties.

RELIABILITY: The probability that a structure will fulfill its design purpose.

RETURN PERIOD: Average interval of time in years between exceedances of an event magnitude.

RISK: The probability of failure or one minus the reliability. Also it is sometimes defined as the probability weighted consequence of failure.

SAFETY INDEX: (Also known as beta value.) A measure of relative structural reliability inherent in a safety check. Beta provides the number of standard deviations that the mean safety margin is located from a point of failure. It is efficiently found from a Level II - advanced first order second moment computer program which incorporates probability distributions of random variables. Beta is reasonably correlated with the reliability magnitude (using a normal probability table) that would be found if the reliability were calculated from repeated simulations of the safety margin. Higher values of beta indicate greater reliability. (A safety index value of beta equal to 3.0 corresponds closely to a 999 out of 1000 reliability or one in a thousand risk.

STANDARD DEVIATION: The positive square root of the weighted average of the squared deviation from the mean. It is the square root of the variance and is a measure of the dispersion of a random variable.

WORKING STRESS DESIGN (WSD): This traditional design format uses nominal loads (unfactored) and compares the stresses produced by these loads with an allowable or working stress level. The latter is obtained by dividing the material yield stress by a factor of safety.

COMMENTARY A PLANNING

COMM. A.3 OPERATIONAL CONSIDERATIONS

Comm. A.3.8 Wells. If the platform is to be set over an existing well with the wellhead above water, information is needed on the dimensions of the tree, size of conductor pipe, and the elevations of the casing head flange and top of wellhead above mean low water. If the existing well is a temporary subsea completion, plans should be made for locating the well and setting the platform properly so that the well can later be extended above the surface of the water.

COMM. A.4 ENVIRONMENTAL CONSIDERATIONS

Comm. A.4.1 General. Selection of environmental criteria should be made after consultation with both the platform designer and specialists in oceanography, seismology, sea ice, etc. The source of all data should be noted, and the methods employed in developing available data into the desired environmental values should be defined.

Comm. A.4.2 Winds. The wind velocity may be classified as either (1) gusts, which are averages over less than one minute, or (2) sustained wind speeds which are averages over one minute or longer. Wind data should be adjusted to a standard elevation of $10 \, \text{m}$ (33 ft.) above mean water level with a specified averaging time such as one hour. Wind data may be adjusted to any specified averaging time or elevation using standard references. See Section C.3.4. Overland wind measurements should be corrected to reflect overwater conditions. For example, see Reference A3.

The spectrum of wind speed fluctuations about the average should be specified in some instances. For example, compliant structures in deep water may have natural sway periods in the range of one minute, in which there is significant energy in the wind speed fluctuations. The following should be considered in determining appropriate design wind speeds:

For normal conditions:

1. The frequency of occurrence of specified sustained wind speeds from various directions for each month or season.   
2. The persistence of sustained wind speeds above specified thresholds for each month or season.   
3. The probable speed of gusts associated with sustained wind speeds.

For extreme conditions:

Projected extreme wind speeds of specified directions and averaging times as a function of their recurrence

interval should be developed. Data should be given concerning:

1. The measurement site, date of occurrence, magnitude of measured gusts and sustained wind speeds, and wind directions for the recorded wind data used during the development of the projected extreme winds.   
2. The projected number of occasions during the specified life of the structure when sustained wind speeds from specified directions should exceed a specific lower bound wind speed.

Comm. A.4.3 Waves. Experienced specialists knowledgeable in the fields of meteorology, oceanography, and hydrodynamics should be consulted when developing wave-dependent criteria. In those areas where prior knowledge of oceanographic conditions is insufficient, the development of wave-dependent design parameters should include the following steps:

1. Development of all necessary meteorological data.   
2. Projection of surface wind fields.   
3. Prediction of deep water general seastates along storm tracks using a mathematical model.   
4. Definition of maximum possible seastates consistent with geographical limitations.   
5. Delineation of bathymetric effects on deep water seastates.   
6. Introduction of probabilistic techniques to predict seastate occurrences at the platform site against various time bases.   
7. Development of design wave parameters (through physical and economic risk evaluation) to produce loads defined in Sections C.3.2 and C.3.3.

In areas where considerable previous knowledge and experience with oceanographic conditions exist, the foregoing sequence may be shortened to those steps needed to project this past knowledge into the required design parameters.

The platform owner should select the design seastate after considering all of the factors listed in Section A.4. In developing seastate data, consideration should be given to the following:

For normal conditions (for both seas and swells):

1. For each month and/or season, the probability of occurrence and average persistence of various seastates, e.g., waves higher than $3\mathrm{m}$ (10 ft.) from specified directions in terms of general seastate description parameters (e.g., the significant wave height and the average wave period).

2. The wind speeds, tides, currents, and marine growth existing simultaneously with the seastates of Item 1 above.   
3. The percentage of waves having heights, directions, and periods within specified ranges, e.g., 3 to $4\mathrm{m}$ (10 to 12 ft) high waves from SSE $\pm 11.25^{\circ}$ during each month and/or season.

For extreme conditions:

Projected extreme wave heights from specified directions should be developed and presented as a function of their expected average recurrence intervals. Other data which should be developed include:

1. The probable range and distribution of wave periods associated with extreme wave heights.   
2. The projected distribution of other wave heights, maximum crest elevations, and the wave energy spectrum in the seastate producing extreme wave heights.   
3. The tides, currents, winds and marine growth likely to occur simultaneously with the seastate producing the extreme waves.   
4. The nature, date, and place of the event which produced the historical seastates (e.g., Hurricane Camille, August 1969, Gulf of Mexico) used in the development of the projected values.

Comm. A.4.4 Tides. Tides may be classified as (1) astronomical tide, (2) wind tide, and (3) pressure differential tide. The latter two are frequently combined and called storm surge. The sum of the three tides is called the storm tide. In the design of a fixed offshore platform, the storm tide elevation is the datum upon which storm waves are superimposed. The variations in elevations of the daily astronomical tides, however, determine the elevations of the boat landings, the fenders, the splash zone treatment of the steel members, and the upper limits of marine growth.

Comm. A.4.5 Currents. The most common categories of currents are (1) tidal currents (associated with astronomical tides), (2) circulational currents (associated with oceanic scale circulation patterns), and (3) storm-generated currents. The vector sum of these three currents is the total current, and the speed and direction of the current at specified elevations is the current profile. The total current profile associated with the seastate producing the extreme waves should be specified for platform design. The frequency of occurrence of total current speed and direction at different depths for each month and/or season may be useful for planning operations.

Boat landings and fenders should be located, where possible, to allow the boat to engage the platform as it moves against the current.

Comm. A.4.8 Other Oceanographic and Meteorological Information. General information on the various types of storms which might affect the platform site should be used to supplement other data developed for normal conditions. Statistics can be compiled giving the expected occurrence of storms by season, direction of approach, etc. Of special interest for construction planning are the duration, the speed of movement and development, and the extent of these conditions. Also of major importance is the ability to forecast storms in the vicinity of a platform.

Comm. A.4.9.5 Scour. The presence of mobile seabed sandwaves, sandhills and sand ribbons indicates a vigorous natural scour regime. Past bed movement may be evidenced by geophysical contrasts, or by variation in density, grading, color or biological indicators in seabed samples and soundings. Sand or silt soils in water depths less than about $40\mathrm{m}$ (130 ft.) are particularly susceptible to scour, but scour has been observed in cobbles, gravels and clays, and in deeper water, depending on the vigour of currents and waves. Offshore scour phenomena are described in References G96 and G97.

COMM. A.5 SELECTING THE DESIGN CONDITIONS

Consideration of the factors listed in Section A.5 and past experiences for drilling and production platforms in the Gulf of Mexico has led to the establishment of reference design levels (see Section C.3.7). The load and resistance factors recommended in Sections C, D, E, F, G and H are intended for use in designing the structure in accordance with these guidelines; they are not intended for use with other codes of practice.

Where the reference level guidelines are not used, the environmental conditions selected for the platform may be based on a risk analysis. This analysis should include the estimated cost of the platform designed to environmental conditions for several average recurrence intervals; the probability of platform damage or loss when subjected to environmental conditions of various recurrence intervals; the financial loss due to platform damage or loss including lost production, cleanup, platform and well replacement, etc. The safety index reliability approach utilized in the present load and resistance factor design (LRFD) format is reasonable for such risk analysis.

COMMENTARY B DESIGN REQUIREMENTS

COMM. B.2 DESIGN FOR IN-PLACE CONDITIONS

Sections B.2 and B.3 identify all the loading conditions required to be considered in the design. The service life is the intended useful life of the platform.

Except for fatigue, the design requirements of this guideline are the same for platforms of all service lives. For example, the return period and load factor for wind, wave, and current loads are the same whether the platform has a service life of 5 years or 30 years. This assures that all platforms have the same reliability in any single year. This is desirable for the safety of personnel and to control an owner's annual financial risk from the exposure of all his platforms.

During the LRFD Beta calibration process, 20 to 25 years was assumed to be the service life. This assumption is reflected in the 0.7 "bias," the ratio of mean (lifetime maximum) wind-wave-current load to the design 100-year wind-wave-current load. Because the LRFD calibration matched the Beta of current WSD provisions, virtually identical load and resistance factors would have resulted if a 20-, 30-, or 50-year service life had been assumed. (See Reference B1, Table 5.5 for a demonstration of insensitivity of load factor to load bias.)

As one would anticipate, a shorter service life reduces the chance of encountering an extreme environmental event and so increases the lifetime probability of survival. Moses (Reference B2) shows a significant (0.5) increase in lifetime safety index Beta if the service life decreases from 30 to 5 years. For an unmanned platform with untypical field development economics and a shortened service life, the owner may want to take advantage of this phenomenon. However, the change in the design load should be determined by a reliability analysis, and not by picking the return period to be a multiple of the service life. Lloyd (Reference B3) shows that designing a 1-year service life platform for a 5-year return period load results in an annual probability of failure that is 200 times larger (and a lifetime probability of failure 10 times larger) than a 20-year service life platform designed to a 100-year return period load, even though the ratio of return period to service life is five in both cases.

COMM. B.4 THE STRENGTH AND STABILITY CHECK

These provisions use the load and resistance factor design format. In general, different components (tubular members, joints, piles, etc.) have different resistance factors (also called strength reduction factors or $\phi$ factors); different loads (wave, dead load, live load, etc.) have different load factors (also called $\gamma$ factors) which may vary depending on which other loads are combined with them.

The RP2A one-third increase on allowable stresses for load combinations involving environmental loads is no longer used; the load and resistance factors include any adjustments appropriate for environmental or combined loading. The variable $\mathbf{Q}$ has been introduced as the symbol for an internal force or stress due to factored external loads.

COMM.B.5 STRUCTURAL ANALYSIS

In general, load factors are applied to external loads before calculating internal forces. If the structure and support conditions are linear, it does not matter whether the load factor is applied to the external load or the internal force. When nonlinearity exists, applying the load factors to the external loads ensures compatible deformations and equilibrium of internal forces at a load closer to an overload condition.

COMM.B.6 REDUNDANCY

The capacity of offshore structures to safely withstand overload situations is normally significantly greater than the capacity of any single member would imply. Local failures can often be tolerated without endangering the platform. Loads which would normally be supported by such failed structural components can often be transferred and safely sustained by under-stressed, interconnecting members. Under-stressed components (and resulting reserve capacity) could exist in offshore platforms for the following reasons:

1. Inclusion of redundant members in many structural framing systems.   
2. Permanent retention of structural components required to withstand temporary loads (e.g., transportation, launching, and construction loads).   
3. Oversized columns needed to contain large diameter piling.   
4. Inclusion of minimum wall thickness to resist corrosion.   
5. Oversizing members to standard sizes and to reduce the number of different member sizes needed.   
6. Over-design of joints and legs resulting when piles are grouted to legs.   
7. Expediting the design process, e.g., to speed up the design process, designers are often reluctant to eliminate or downsize under-stressed members because every possible loading condition and design requirement would need to be reexamined.

For framing patterns which do not qualify as being similar to those shown to have adequate reserve strength, a nonlinear overload analysis can verify redundancy. Methods, as well as conclusions about superior framing, can be found in Reference B6 through B9.

Comm. B.6.1 Status of System Factor. In the initial LRFD feasibility study for platform design (Reference B4), the advantages of a system factor, $\phi_{s}$ , were pointed out. It would appear directly in the component checking equation as:

$$\phi_{s} \phi_{n} R_{n} > (\Sigma \gamma_{i} F_{n}, i) \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \tag{Comm.B-1}$$

The system factor would reflect the importance of the member to the structure's integrity. The value of the system factor would be based on ductility and redundancy of the structure and consequences of individual member failure.

This initial RP2A-LRFD does not specify any system factors as this is an evolving area of study for which no clear "rules" have emerged, even though system considerations are already implicitly part of design.

In seismic design, adequate framing arrangements may be used to satisfy the ductility check. In addition, system reserves are recognized in consideration of accidental loadings and gross errors in design, fabrication, or construction.

Future versions of RP2A-LRFD may contain explicit system factors for component design. Such system factors would likely carry certain other requirements, e.g., X-bracing, adequate horizontal load transfer, minimum D/t and KL/r ratios to assure ductility, adequate joint capacity, etc. Smaller system factors would be appropriate for critical, nonredundant components.

The development of general purpose system factors would require an extensive study. Nonlinear overload

analysis of various platform geometries and a rational multiple-failure-mode, systems-reliability methodology will be required. An outline of the requirements for such a study is given in Section 8.5 of Reference B5.

COMM. B.8 DEFORMATION LOADS. In general, the ultimate strengths of ductile structural systems are not sensitive to deformation loads. Behavior of ductile components beyond full plastic loading are not affected by the initial level of internal stressing. Where deformation loads become particularly important is where subsequent loading may be cyclic and cause repeated plastic deformation. In such cases, fatigue damage could occur. Deformation load conditions should therefore be checked on a case-by-case basis. Components must be checked to ensure that they can deform plastically (without buckling) and that the loads do not cause fatigue damage. If these conditions can be demonstrated, then deformation loads do not need to be included in the component strength checking.

If it is determined that deformation loads must be considered, then they should be included in Equations C.2-1, C.3-1, C.3-2, C.3-3, C.4-1, and C.4-2 as follows:

D1 Dead Load prestressing, creep/relaxation, settlement.   
D2 Dead Load permanent temperature loads (air, seawater).   
L1 Live Load production oriented temperature loads.

COMMENTARY C LOADS

COMM.C.1 SCOPE

The load factors in Section C are intended to cover variations in external load intensity from the specified nominal values, and the uncertainties inherent in predicting internal member forces. The values have been primarily calibrated to conditions experienced in the Gulf of Mexico accounting for the analysis procedures normally followed in applying 15th edition RP2A recommended practice. The calibration process is very robust and should still be valid for the changes incorporated in the 20th edition.

In no instance should load factors be used as a substitute for rational analysis, e.g., to account for dynamics.

In instances where load factors are not prescribed here, or additional performance or test data are available, then an appropriate reliability analysis should be carried out. Load factors should be derived from a reliability analysis that includes uncertainty in selecting load intensity; probability of simultaneous occurrence of independent loads; accuracy of load effect (internal force) prediction; and interpretation of relevant field experience, verification, and control. Acceptable reliability should be based on failure consequences and compatibility with target reliabilities for other load cases that are covered by this practice.

In lieu of a detailed reliability analysis, the following simplified procedure should produce acceptable design values for loads acting alone. For a new load, S, one needs to determine the mean value of its lifetime maximum, $\bar{\mathbf{S}}$ . Also, one needs the bias, $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{s}}$ , which is the ratio of the mean value, $\bar{\mathbf{S}}$ , to the nominal or design value, $\mathbf{S}_{\mathrm{n}}$ . Finally, one needs the coefficient of variation of the load, $\mathbf{V}_{\mathrm{s}}$ , considering both the intensity and analysis uncertainty. From Table Comm C.1-1, select a mean load factor $\bar{\gamma}$ and multiply it by the bias, $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{s}}$ , to obtain the load factor $\gamma^{*}$ . For example, wave load has been modeled by $\mathbf{V}_{\mathrm{s}}$ of 0.37 and a bias $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{s}} = 0.70$ ; Table Comm C.1-1 gives a load factor $\gamma^{*} = (1.99)(0.70) = 1.39$ , close to the value given in Section C.3.1.1. Using the resistance factors provided in this document and Table Comm C.1-1 results in a safety index consistent with other safety indices in this document.

Comm. C.2.1 Factored Gravity Loads. These load factors were determined through a calibration process that also included wind, wave and current loads. No distinction was made between $\mathbf{D}_1$ and $\mathbf{D}_2$ , or $\mathbf{L}_1$ and $\mathbf{L}_2$ , so the load factors are the same. Nevertheless, it is useful to establish these subsets in which the loads have common degrees of uncertainty and duration of occurrence.

The choice of 1.3 on dead load and 1.5 on live load results in a larger safety index than WSD practice for components with both environmental and gravity loading. While the reliability concept of uniform safety could justify lower factors, the results would be a wide departure from past practice. The ANSI recommenda

tions in Reference C1 include the same conservative approach for this problem.

The safety index calibration used the following statistical model: $\mathbf{L}_1$ and $\mathbf{L}_2$ have a COV of $14\%$ and the mean value is the nominal value. $\mathbf{D}_1$ and $\mathbf{D}_2$ have a COV of $8\%$ and the mean value is the nominal value. For the calibration, the internal force due to gravity load was assumed to be $75\% (\mathbf{L}_1 + \mathbf{L}_2)$ and $25\% (\mathbf{D}_1 + \mathbf{D}_2)$ .

Comm. C.2.3 Dead Load 2, $\mathbf{D}_2$ . This category has been separated from traditional live loads because there is little variability in its magnitude when the equipment or package is known.

Comm. C.2.6 Unintentional Flooding. As noted in Section C.2.2, buoyancy (and hydrostatic pressure) is considered to be a Dead Load 1. This is consistent with the relatively high certainty of the displaced volume of a member. In some computer analyses, buoyancy forces are computed as part of the wave pressure; the intention of this section should be followed, and some programming modifications may be necessary to allow for the use of different load factors on buoyancy loads and wave loads.

One unique uncertainty in the buoyancy force is whether the member remains unflooded. The occurrence of unintentional flooding is not well documented, so rather than developing an ad hoc load factor, several additional checks are called for. The check of unflooded members as flooded can be done for all members at once, rather than each singly. For intentionally flooded members, the need to assure positive flooding can be critical to prevent hydrostatic collapse, particularly during rapid submergence that may occur during installation. The requirement for flooding some fraction of all unflooded members can be modeled by a set of equivalent joint loads. While no statistics are available, the load should correspond to a reasonable fraction based on the designer's judgment of the long-term effects of corrosion, small wormholes (small-sized porosities) in the welds, and possible design omissions.

COMM. C.3 WIND, WAVE AND CURRENT LOADS

Comm. C.3.1 Strength Requirements. The load factors in Equations C.3-1 and C.3-2 are from the reliability calibration that considered wind, wave and current loads, gravity loads and the strengths of various components.

Equation C.3-1 excludes $\mathbf{L}_2$ due to its short duration and small probability of occurring simultaneously with a storm.

Equation C.3-2 covers the situation of counteracting loads when two nominal internal forces are similar in magnitude but opposite in sign. The algebraic sum of the forces is small which leads to a small required resistance. Due to the greater uncertainties in environmental loads, the safety index beta can be low (high risk). This phenomena is intensified when the component capacity is different with changes in the sign of the loading (e.g., piles in tension vs. compression or axial members in compression vs. tension).

In the LRFD calibration, counteracting loads were considered an important load condition for uplift on piles. The reduced load factors in Equation C.3-2 compared to C.3-1 assure adequate pile tension capacity. A reduced factor on $\mathbf{D}_2$ and $\mathbf{L}_2$ implicitly covers cases of reduced deck load. The 0.8 on $\mathbf{L}_1$ is smaller than the 0.9 on $\mathbf{D}_2$ , reflecting its greater likelihood of not being present to the value assumed. However, reductions are even applied to the very certain and always present $\mathbf{D}_1$ , because it is the uncertainty in wind, wave and current that this check is intended to guard against. The safety index is hereby raised to a level consistent with the pile compression failure mode.

For platform brace members, an analogous case of counteracting loads exists. A calibration platform (Platform "C") was investigated for this phenomena by looking at the most critical component in each design group (Reference C2). While the load factors in Equation C.3-1 alone serve to raise Beta compared to WSD for opposing load cases, it was deemed prudent to have Equation C.3-2 apply to all platform components to guard against low Beta cases.

Comm. C.3.1.2. Extreme Wind, Wave and Current Load, $\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{e}}$ . Return period means the average interval of time between exceedances of the magnitude of an event. In the following discussion, a 100-year event is used consistently as the extreme event for design, recognizing that for some situations another return period may be more appropriate.

Three possibilities were carefully examined for defining the combined extreme wind, wave, and current load, $\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{e}}$ .

1. 100-yr. return period wave height with "associated" wind and "associated" current;   
2. Any "reasonable" combination of wind speed, wave height, and current speed that results in the 100-yr.

return period combined platform load, e.g., base shear or base overturning moment. This is a deterministically calculated load based on the joint statistics of the environmental parameters. It does not contain uncertainties in loads caused by scatter in drag and inertial coefficients, deviations of actual ocean wave profiles from theoretical wave profiles used for design, etc.; and

3. 100-yr. return period wave height combined with the 100-yr. return period wind speed and the 100-yr. return period current speed.

After considering the technical and practical merits of each of the three definitions, Definition 1 was selected for this RP2A-LRFD. The following paragraphs discuss each of the definitions as they apply to defining the combined $\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{e}}$ for storm-generated events. Special considerations and applicability of these definitions for locations where tidal and/or general circulation currents such as the Loop current and the Gulf Stream are important are discussed in the last paragraph of this commentary section.

Definition 1 has been the traditional definition in the RP2A-WSD. The words "associated wind and current" have always been included, and the 100-yr. return period wave height is specified for design use in Table C.3.7-1 and in Figure C.3.7-3 for the Gulf of Mexico. A problem with Definition 1 is that the meaning of "associated" is somewhat ambiguous. One interpretation of "associated" is the statistically expected value of current or wind coexisting with the 100-yr. return period wave height. For structures dominated by wave loads, use of these expected values will result in an adequate design load. This wave-dominance will apply to almost all of the structures covered by this RP2A-LRFD. For structures dominated by either wind or current loads, one should at least check the structure for the 100-yr. return period wind or current combination in conjunction with the associated wave height. For structures where more than one environmental parameter is important, a special study should be undertaken using the joint statistics of the parameters to arrive at the combination yielding approximately the 100-yr. return period load. Definition 2 could then be used to obtain the design load. In lieu of such a study, Definition 3 could be used to obtain a conservative value of the design load.

Definition 3 was initially chosen as the basic definition. It is precise, independent of the structure, and can be determined from separate (marginal) statistics of waves, currents and wind. This definition will always yield results that are conservative and in some cases may be too conservative.

Definition 2 will result in a lower load than Definition 3, especially if the interdependence among waves, winds, and currents is weak. If the interdependence is strong, this definition could still result in lower loads than Definition 3 if differences in direction between winds, waves and currents and differences in time of

occurrence of peak winds, waves, and currents during the storm are modeled. However, in using Definition 2, one should not just use any combination of wave, wind, and current that satisfies the 100-yr. return period response, but should make a "reasonable" choice so as to model the probable spatial load distribution over the structure.

Additional considerations must be given to obtaining $\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{e}}$ for locations where either tidal or general circulation currents, such as the Loop current and the Gulf Stream, are important. Definition 1 would be acceptable if the storm-generated conditions were the predominant contributors to the extreme load, and if one could determine the appropriate "associated" value of tidal and circulation current. Definition 2 is more general and could be used to obtain $\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{e}}$ that includes the effects of currents of nonstorm origin. The most direct way to obtain data for use with Definition 2 would be to perform simulations of the environment in which realizations of the load stochastic processes could be used to back out probable combinations of wave height, wind speed, and the various current components that produce the 100-yr. return period load. Definition 2 would provide an adequate assessment of the combined extreme design load and would provide an adequate load even for wind and current sensitive structures. However, the results would be structure dependent and consequently separate simulations may be required for each structure. Definition 3 will assure an adequate design load (but it will be conservative with respect to the 100-yr. return period load) for any structure and will require the least amount of work. However, for design of structures that are subjected to strong currents of nonstorm origin, such as the Gulf Stream currents, Definition 3 may yield combined extreme loads that are too conservative.

Comm. C.3.1.4 Operating Wind, Wave and Current Load. The operating wind, wave and current conditions should be representative of moderately severe conditions at the platform. They should not necessarily be limiting conditions which, if exceeded, require the cessation of platform operations. Typically, a 1-year to 5-year winter storm is used as an operating wind, wave and current condition in the Gulf of Mexico.

"Operating environmental conditions" combined with gravity loads (and without a one-third allowable stress increase) has been a loading condition in RP2A-WSD since the first edition. This recognizes that some wave, wind and current load will certainly be present with the maximum gravity loads. An operating strength check was continued in LRFD for this reason and because it is part of current Gulf of Mexico practice.

Unlike extreme wind, wave and current, the operating wind, wave and current load in LRFD was intentionally not tied to a specific return period event. The Beta calibration was done without making use of the operating wind-wave-current case. The use of Equation C.3-3 with $\mathbf{W}_0$ corresponding to "moderately severe condi

tions" in the Gulf of Mexico adds a small but uncalibrated increment to member size and safety for members loaded principally by gravity loads. Outside the Gulf of Mexico, if "moderately severe conditions" are defined as the same return period event, Equation C.3-3 may be conservative beyond the original intention. Be aware that (as some formula comparisons will demonstrate) Equation C.3-3 will produce smaller design forces compared to RP2A-WSD for certain ranges of loads, namely those members subjected to mostly (but not $100\%$ ) gravity load and an operating wave load $\mathbf{W}_0$ that exceeds about one half $\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{e}}$ .

The load factor of 1.2 was selected to cover the analysis uncertainty (of applying loads and computing stresses) that is part of all load factors. Since the operational wind-wave-current check is not checking safety for unusual environmental loads but rather primarily for gravity loads, a factor less than 1.35 is appropriate. Note that the check for gravity load effects opposing wave load effects has been omitted. It is not necessary since the goal of avoiding low safety when a gravity load opposes a more uncertain environmental load is achieved by Equation C.3-2.

Comm. C.3.2.1 Apparent Wave Period. Reference C271 contains a consistent first-order solution for the apparent wave period of a wave propagating on a current with an arbitrary profile. Their procedure requires the solution of the following three simultaneous equations for $\mathbf{T}_{\mathrm{app}},\lambda ,$ and $\mathbf{V_I}$ ..

$$\begin{array}{l} \frac{\lambda}{T} \quad = \frac{\lambda}{T_{\text{a p p}}} + V_{I} \\ T_{\text{a p p}}^{2} = \frac{2 \pi \lambda}{g \tanh  (2 \pi d / \lambda)} \\ \mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{I}} = \frac{(4 \pi / \lambda)}{\sinh (4 \pi \mathrm{d} / \lambda)} \int_{- \mathrm{d}}^{0} \mathrm{U}_{\mathrm{c}} (\mathrm{z}) \cosh \left[ \frac{4 \pi (\mathrm{z} + \mathrm{d})}{\lambda} \right] \mathrm{d z} \\ \end{array}$$

Here, $\lambda$ is wave length, $\mathbf{T}$ is the wave period seen by a stationary observer, $\mathrm{T_{app}}$ is the wave period seen by an observer moving at the effective in-line current speed $\mathbf{V}_{\mathrm{I}},\mathbf{g}$ is the acceleration due to gravity, $\mathbf{U}_{\mathbf{c}}(\mathbf{z})$ is the component of the steady current profile at elevation $\mathbf{z}$ (positive above storm mean level) in the wave direction, and $\mathbf{d}$ is storm water depth. For the special case of a uniform current profile, the solution to these equations is provided in dimensionless form in Figure C.3.2-2.

Comm. C.3.2.2 Two-Dimensional Wave Kinematics. There are several wave theories that can be used to predict the kinematics of the two-dimensional, regular waves used for static, deterministic wave load calculations. The different theories all provide approximate solutions to the same differential equation and boundary conditions. All compute a wave that is symmetric about the crest and propagates without changing shape. They differ in their functional formulation and in the

degree to which they satisfy the nonlinear kinematic and dynamic boundary conditions at the surface of the wave.

Linear wave theory is applicable only when the linearization of the free surface boundary conditions is reasonable, i.e., when the wave amplitude and steepness are infinitesimal. Stokes V (Reference C306) is a fifth order expansion about mean water level and satisfies the free surface boundary conditions with acceptable accuracy over a fairly broad range of applications, as shown in Figure C.3.2.3 Atkins (1990), Reference C252. Chappel's theory (Reference C309) is similar to Stokes V but determines the coefficients in the expansion numerically, through a least squares minimization of errors in the free surface boundary conditions, rather than analytically. EXVP-D (Reference C273) satisfies the dynamic boundary condition exactly and minimizes the errors in the kinematic boundary condition. Stream Function theory (Reference C259) satisfies the kinematic boundary condition exactly and minimizes the errors in the dynamic boundary. When Stokes V theory is not applicable, higher-order Chappel, EXVP-D, or Stream Function theory may be used. Of these, the most broadly used is Stream Function. Selection of the appropriate solution order can be based on either the percentage error in the dynamic boundary condition or the percentage change in velocity or acceleration in going to the next higher order. These two methods select comparable solution orders over most of the feasible domain but differ in the extremes of $\mathrm{H} > 0.9\mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{b}}$ and $\mathrm{d / gT_{app}}^2 < 0.003$ . In these extremes, the theory has not been well substantiated with laboratory measurements, and should therefore be used with caution. In particular, the curve for breaking wave height $\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{b}}$ shown in Figure C.3.2-3 is not universally accepted.

Comm. C.3.2.3 Wave Kinematics Factor. In wave force computations with regular waves, the kinematics are computed assuming a unidirectional sea (long-crested waves all propagating in the same direction), whereas the real sea surface is comprised of short-crested, directional waves. In fact, the sea surface can be viewed as the superposition of many small individual wavelets, each with its own amplitude, frequency, and direction of propagation. Fortunately, the directional spreading of the waves tends to result in peak forces that are somewhat smaller than those predicted from unidirectional seas. This force reduction due to directional spreading can be accommodated in static, deterministic wave force design procedures by reducing the horizontal velocity and acceleration from a two-dimensional wave theory by a "spreading factor."

There is generally much less directional spreading for wave frequencies near the peak of the wave spectrum than for higher frequencies (Reference C261, for example). Since the kinematics of the large, well-formed individual waves used in static design are dominated by the most energetic wave frequencies, it is appropriate to use a "spreading factor" corresponding to the spectral peak period. Use of a weighted average spreading factor over all the wave frequencies in the spectrum

would be unconservative. The spreading factor can be estimated either from measured or hindcast directional spectral wave data as $\sqrt{(n+1)/(n+2)}$ , where $n$ is the exponent in the $\cos^n\theta$ spreading function at the spectral peak frequency. Note that measured directional data from pitch/roll buoys tend to significantly overestimate spreading, while directional data from a two-horizontal-axis particle velocimeter are thought to provide a good estimate of spreading.

There is some evidence that, even in seastates with very little directional spreading, two-dimensional Stream Function or Stokes V theory overpredicts the fluid velocities and accelerations (Reference C292). This may be attributed to the irregularity of the real wave, i.e., its front-to-back asymmetry about the wave crest and its change in shape as it propagates. If an "irregularity factor" less than unity is supported by high quality wave kinematics data, including measurements in the crest region above mean water level, appropriate for the types of design-level seastates that the platform may experience, then the "spreading factor" can be multiplied by the "irregularity factor" to get an overall reduction factor for horizontal velocity and acceleration.

Comm. C.3.2.4 Current Blockage Factor. No space-frame or lattice-type structure is totally transparent to waves and current. In other words, all structures cause a global distortion of the incident waves and current in and around the structure. Since global load for space-frame structures is calculated by summing individual member forces, it is important that the local incident flow used to calculate local member forces in Morison's equation account for global distortion effects.

Space-frame structures distort the waves as well as the current. References C291 and C264, for example, address the reduction in wave amplitude across arrays of vertical cylinders. Some field data indicate that the rms orbital velocity very near the platform is slightly reduced from that at several platform widths upwave. However, this reduction is not evident in all the data. Until more evidence to the contrary is accumulated, it is appropriate to continue with the assumption that a typical space-frame platform does not significantly distort the incident wave kinematics in a global sense.

For currents, however, there now exists a substantial body of evidence that supports a reduction in the current within the platform space-frame relative to the freestream current. Laboratory and field data indicate that the blockage factor can be as low as 0.6 for a structure as dense as the Lena guyed tower (References C272, C294 and C295); about 0.7 for a typical compliant tower (Reference C280); and about 0.75 to 0.85 for a typical jacket (Reference C251). Figure Comm. C.3.2.4 shows the measured current field at $18\mathrm{m}$ (60 ft) depth around and through the Bullwinkle platform in a Loop Current event in 1991. The average blockage factor within the platform computed from the data is 0.77.

The blockage factor for steady current can be estimated from the "actuator disk" model Reference C297 as

$$[ 1 + \Sigma (\mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{d}} \mathrm{A})_{\mathrm{i}} / 4 \overline{{\mathrm{A}}} ]^{-1}$$

![](API_RP_2A-LRFD_1st/chunk2_031ff94fd2a1953ab75dd85cbf03263bd34f21254bb4f51ce3c840ba23c7dc88.jpg)  
FIG.COMM.C.3.2.4  
CURRENT VECTORS COMPUTED FROM DOPPLER MEASUREMENTS  
AT 18M (60 FT.) ON THE BULLWINKLE PLATFORM (100 CM/S

where $\Sigma (\mathbf{C_dA})_j$ is the summation of the "drag areas" of all the members (including horizontals) in the flow, and $\tilde{\mathbf{A}}$ is the area within the perimeter area of the platform projected normal to the current. For structures where geometry changes significantly with depth, the blockage factor can be computed for different depth levels. If the calculated reduction factor is less than 0.7, consideration should be given to modeling the platform as a series of actuator disks rather than a single actuator disk. Other limitations of the actuator disk model are discussed in Reference C297.

An alternative expression for the blockage factor based on a similar approach to Taylor's but accounting for mixing downstream, is given in Reference C275. In the case of small values of the ratio $\Sigma (\mathrm{C_qA})_i / \overline{\mathbf{A}}$ , the alternative expression reduces to Taylor's. Lambrakos and Beckmann also give expressions for treating the jacket and conductor group separately.

The global "blockage" discussed here, and the "shielding" discussed in Comm. C.3.2.8 are related. In fact, Reference C272 uses the term "shielding" instead of the term "blockage" to describe the current speed reduction. The term interference has also been used in discussions of these phenomena. For present purposes, the term "shielding" is used only in reference to members in the local wake of neighboring members (like conductor arrays), and the "shielding factor" is to be applied to the calculated loads due to both waves and currents. The term "blockage" is used in reference to the entire structure, and the "blockage factor" is to be applied to the far-field current speed only. With this distinction, one would first use the blockage factor to calculate a reduced current speed for the entire structure. The reduced current speed and undisturbed wave kinematics would be used in Morison's equation to calculate local loads on all members. The calculated loads on conductors would then be reduced by the shielding factor.

Comm. C.3.2.5 Combined Wave/Current Kinematics. References C258 and C260 show that waves alternately stretch and compress the current profile under crests and troughs, respectively. Reference C258 found that a model that combined Doppler-shifted wave kinematics with a nonlinearly stretched current profile gave the best estimate of global loads on a structure. Nonlinear stretching computes the stretched current for a particle instantaneously at elevation $z$ as the speed $U_{c}(z')$ evaluated from the specified current profile at elevation $z'$ , the mean elevation of the particle over a full wave cycle. The elevations $z$ and $z'$ are related through linear (Airy) wave theory as follows:

$$z = z^{\prime} + \eta \frac{\sinh (2 \pi (z^{\prime} + d) / \lambda_{n})}{\sinh (2 \pi d / \lambda_{n})}$$

Here, $\mathbf{d}$ is storm water depth, $\eta$ is the wave surface directly above the water particle, and $\lambda_{n}$ is the wave length determined from nonlinear wave theory for a wave of height $H$ and period $T_{app}$ . The elevations $z$ , $z'$ , and $\eta$ are all positive above storm mean water level.

This equation gives a nonlinear stretching of the current, with the greatest stretching occurring high in the water column, where the particle orbits have the greatest radii. The nonlinearly stretched current profile, coupled with Doppler shifted wave kinematics, produces global platform loads that are within $+1$ to $-4$ percent of those produced by the exact solution on a typical drag-dominant structure subjected to representative waves and current profiles.

Another acceptable approximate model for many applications is one that uses a linearly stretched current profile, with

$$z + d = \left(z^{\prime} + d\right) (d + \eta) / d$$

The stretched current profiles from the two models are compared qualitatively in Figure Comm. C.3.2.5 for typical sheared and slab current profiles under a wave crest. The linearly stretched current produces global loads on a typical drag-dominant platform that are nearly as accurate as those produced by the nonlinearly stretched current, being within 0 to -6 percent of loads produced by the exact solution. However, it does not simulate the combined wave/current velocity profile from the exact solution as faithfully as nonlinear stretching.

Vertical extrapolation of the input current profile above mean water level produces reasonably accurate estimates of global loads on drag-dominant platforms in most cases. In particular, for a slab profile thicker than about $50\mathrm{m}$ (164 ft.) like the recommended profiles in Section C.3.7, vertical extrapolation produces nearly the same result as nonlinear stretching, as illustrated in Figure Comm. C.3.2.5. However, if the specified profile $\mathbf{U}_{\mathbf{c}}$ (z) has a very high speed at mean water level, sheared to much lower speeds just below mean water level, the global force may be overestimated (by about 8 percent in a typical application).

Another approximate model is the linearly stretched model described above, adjusted so that the total momentum in the stretched profile from the seafloor to the wave surface equals that in the specified profile from the seafloor to mean water level. This procedure is not supported by the theoretical analyses in References C258 and C260.

If the current is not in the same direction as the wave, the methods discussed above may still be used, with one modification. Both the in-line and normal components of current would be stretched, but only the in-line component would be used to estimate $\mathrm{T_{app}}$ for the Doppler-shifted wave.

While no exact solution has been developed for irregular waves, the wave/current solution for regular waves can be logically extended. In the first two approximations described above for regular waves, the period and length of the regular wave would be replaced with the period and length corresponding to the spectral peak frequency.
