EXAMPLE STRUCTURE

This factor, D, is appropriate for values of damping between 2 and 10 percent.

Comm. C.4.2.4 Response Analysis. Section C.4.2.4 suggests that the complete quadratic combination (CQC) (Reference C420) of individual modal responses is appropriate for the evaluation of design response. This method accounts for correlation among responses of closely spaced modes. Other combinations may be appropriate for the evaluation of design response. The modal combination rule appropriate for a particular class of structures or members may be evaluated by comparing the response of the structure to a limited number of time histories with its response to the corresponding response spectra (References C458, C459, C460). It is also important to define the proper response variable in applying the response spectrum method. Note that the response variable such as member force is not necessarily the variable that will be directly compared to criteria such as allowable stress.

All of the modes need not be included to obtain an adequate representation of the structural response. The requirement for an adequate representation of the response will normally be met if the extracted modes are selected on the basis of modal parameters such as mass participation factor or a major response parameter such as base shear or energy (References C421, C422). Additional modes may be required if local member effects are important. However, the dynamic response of subassemblage and individual members may require separate consideration.

Comm. C.4.2.5 Response Assessment. In the response spectrum analysis method, the response quantity of interest should be computed separately for each mode and then the modal responses combined using an appropriate method. For example, member end reactions are computed for each mode and combined to obtain the total earthquake induced forces. It should be noted that combining the modal values of actual-to-allowable strength ratios would not be conservative for columns because of the moment amplification term in the allowable strength evaluation.

The total design force for each member is obtained by combining the earthquake induced forces together with forces due to gravity, buoyancy, and hydrostatic loading. In combining the earthquake induced member forces with static forces, account should be taken of the fact that the former have no sense of direction attached to them, and that earthquake induced forces are cyclic in nature. In general, the relative signs of the earthquake related forces acting on a member should be selected such that the most conservative condition will result. However, some unwarranted conservatism may be reduced by rational arguments concerning the expected member behavior such as the type of curvature.

In computing the earthquake induced forces for member design, consideration should also be given to the inertia forces introduced by the local vibrational characteristics of individual members.

Comm. C.4.3 Ductility Requirements

Comm. C.4.3.1 General. In seismically active areas, platform responses to rare, intense earthquake motions may involve inelastic action, and structural damage may occur. The provisions of Sections C.4.3.1 and Comm. C.4.3.1 are intended to ensure that structure-foundation systems planned for such areas remain stable in the event of a rare, intense earthquake at the site. This can be achieved by providing sufficient system redundancy such that load redistribution and inelastic deformation will occur before collapse and by minimizing abrupt changes in stiffness in the vertical configuration of the structure. Adequate ductility can be demonstrated by adhering to the design practices outlined below or by nonlinear analysis, where applicable.

Comm. C.4.3.2 Structures Not Requiring Ductility Analysis. Considerable experience has been developed in recent years in the analysis of the overload performance of conventional structure-pile systems (References C410, C414, C439). Such systems are jacket type structures with eight or more legs; supported by piles in competent soils whose local strength and stiffness degradation under extreme cyclic loading does not significantly compromise the overall integrity of the platform foundation; and located in areas where the intensity ratio of the rare, intense ground motions to the strength level ground motions is approximately 2.0. Based on this experience, the design guidelines of Section C.4.3.2 have been developed (Reference C440). Implementation of these guidelines in the design of similar structures should ensure sufficient ductility for the overload condition. Explicit analysis of the overload performance of such structures should not be necessary.

The guidelines include provisions for configuring and proportioning members in the vertical frames. Their purpose is to provide for redistribution of the horizontal shear loads in the vertical frames as buckling occurs in diagonal bracing, and to improve the post-buckling behavior of the diagonal braces and of nontubular members at connections. These provisions will enhance ductile behavior of the structure under extreme lateral cyclic loading. Figure Comm. C.4.3-1 shows examples of vertical frame configurations which do not meet the guidelines. Example configurations which do meet the guidelines are shown in Figure Comm. C.4.3-2. Note that the two "K" braced panels forming an "X" in two vertically adjacent panels meet the guidelines.

Comm. C.4.3.3 Structures Requiring Ductility Analysis. Reasons that a structure-foundation system may merit an explicit analysis of its performance during a rare, intense earthquake include:

- The seismicity of the site does not conform to the 1:2 ratio of strength to extreme level earthquake ground motion intensities common to offshore southern California. In other areas, this ratio may be higher.   
The pile-supporting soils at the site are susceptible to significant strength and stiffness degradation

FIG.COMM.C.4.3-1 VERTICAL FRAME CONFIGURATIONS NOT MEETING GUIDELINES

![](API_RP_2A-LRFD_1st/chunk2_abf138b1248f13b571086cb87c5ebe329ad31ca4ef8df90e6053f109fca216fc.jpg)  
FIG.COMM.C.4.3-2 VERTICAL FRAME CONFIGURATIONS MEETING GUIDELINES

under the cyclic loadings imposed by a rare, intense earthquake.

- The configuration of the structure (bracing type, member size, D/t and slenderness ratios) does not conform to the structural configurations typical of recently installed earthquake resistant platforms, from which the guidelines of Section C.4.3.2 have been developed.

In order to demonstrate the satisfactory overload performance of these systems, it is necessary to establish appropriate performance criteria, develop representative platform and foundation models, and perform analyses using a method of analysis that reasonably reflects the anticipated response of the platform and its foundation to rare, intense earthquake ground motion (References C417, C418, C439, C441).

Representative sets of ground motion time histories that are characteristic of a rare, intense earthquake at the site should be developed from a site-specific seismic hazard study following the provisions of Section C.4.1.2 and Comm. C.4.1.2. It should be demonstrated that the structure-foundation system remains stable under the loads imposed by these ground motions. The structure-foundation system may be considered unstable when the deflections are large enough to cause collapse under the influence of gravity loads.

The post-yield and post-buckling behavior of structural members subject to overload under cyclic load reversals should be modeled (References C415, C425, C442, C443, C444, C445, C446). For members required to develop significant bending, the interaction between axial load and moment capacity should be included (e.g., deck girders, jacket legs, and piles) (Reference C447). The ductility and cyclic degradation characteristics of tubular members are strongly dependent on their D/t and slenderness ratios (Reference C448). A significant amount of ductility can be built into the structure by implementation of the generic design guidelines presented in Section C.4.3.2. Foundation models should consider the effects of cyclic load reversals, strain rate, pore water pressure generation on the strength and stiffness of the soils surrounding the piles (References C449, C450, C451, C452, C453), and energy dissipation mechanisms (References C454, C455, C456).

The designer should develop a thorough insight into the performance of the structure and foundation during a rare, intense earthquake. The time history method of analysis is recommended. The structure-foundation response should be determined to multiple sets of ground motions which characterize the likely envelope of ground motion intensity, frequency content, phasing and duration expected at the site. At least three sets of representative earthquake ground motion time histories should be analyzed. Additional more simplistic methods of analysis may be used to complement the results of time history analysis (Reference C413).

Comm. C.4.4 Additional Guidelines

Comm. C.4.4.1 Tubular Joints. Joints are sized for the yield or buckling capacity of incoming members so that premature failure of the joints will be avoided and the ductility of the overall structure can be fully developed.

The recommended practice is to size jacket leg joint cans for full yield in main diagonals and for the buckling load of principal horizontals. These horizontals typically have small loads for elastic analysis but are required to pick up substantial compressive loads to prevent the structure from "unzipping" after main diagonals buckle. Excessive joint can thickness may often be avoided by using a conical stub end of the governing member, or by considering the beneficial effects of member overlap and/or grouted-in piles.

Comm. C.4.4.2 Deck Appurtenances and Equipment. The method of deriving seismic design forces for a deck appurtenance depends upon the appurtenance's dynamic characteristics and framing complexity. There are two analysis alternatives.

First, through proper anchorage and lateral restraint, most deck equipment and piping are sufficiently stiff such that their support framing, lateral restraint framing, and anchorage can be designed using static forces derived from peak deck accelerations associated with the strength level seismic event.

To provide assurance that the appurtenance is sufficiently stiff to meet this criterion, the lateral and vertical periods of the appurtenance should be located on the low period, 'flat' portion of the deck level floor response spectra. Additionally, the local framing of the deck that supports the appurtenance must also be rigid enough to not introduce dynamic amplification effects. In selecting the design lateral acceleration values, consideration should be given to the increased response towards the corners of the deck caused by the torsional response of the platform.

Second, in cases of more compliant equipment - such as drilling and well servicing structures, flare booms, cranes, deck cantilevers, tall free-standing vessels, unbaffled tanks with free fluid surfaces, long-spanning risers and flexible piping, escape capsules, and wellhead/manifold interaction - consideration should be given to accommodating the additional stresses caused by dynamic amplification and/or differential displacements estimated through either coupled or decoupled analyses.

Decoupled analyses using deck floor spectra are likely to produce greater design loads on equipment than those derived using a more representative coupled analysis. This is particularly the case for more massive components, especially those with natural periods close to the significant natural periods of the platform. References C461 through C464 describe coupled procedures, and decoupled procedures which attempt to account for such interaction.

If coupled analyses are used on relatively rigid components that are modelled simplistically, care should be exercised such that the design accelerations which are derived from the modal combination procedure are not less than the peak deck accelerations.

Field inspection by experienced personnel of equipment and piping on existing platforms in seismic areas can help identify equipment anchorage and restraint that by experience and/or analysis should be upgraded. To accommodate loadings and/or differential displacements, the addition or deletion of simple bracing and/or anchorage to these components can significantly improve their performance during an earthquake. This is especially important for critical components such as piping and vessels handling hazardous materials, emergency battery racks, process control equipment, etc.

The use of a higher strength level earthquake load factor is usually appropriate for designing deck supported structures, local deck framing, equipment anchorage, and lateral restraint framing under strength level earthquake loads. This higher load factor is intended to provide a margin of safety in lieu of performing an explicit ductility level analysis.

However, in areas where the ratio of rare, intense ground motion intensities to strength level ground motion intensities is known to be higher than 2.0, an adjustment to the strength level earthquake load factor should be considered. Also, for certain equipment, piping, appurtenances or supporting structures, the degree of redundancy, consequences of failure and/or metallurgy may dictate the use of different strength level earthquake load factors or a full ductility analysis, depending on the component's anticipated performance under rare, intense earthquake ground motions.

COMM. C.5 FABRICATION AND INSTALLATION LOADS

Comm. C.5.1 General. Construction and installation loads and corresponding safety checks are often ignored in most codes because these consequences are viewed as owner risks and do not affect the general public. For platforms, failures during this phase are primarily economic and may not involve operating personnel or environmental hazards. The situation changes, however, if structures are partially damaged during the construction and installation phase and this fact escapes detection. Subsequent capacity to perform functions or resist environmental hazards may be reduced. Consequently, RP2A has considered such loads.

Installation loads take on a number of characteristics that may be different from operating and environmental loads. In particular, during the installation stage the structure is in an equilibrium balance such that arbitrary use of load factors can lead to incorrect and even unsafe results. Unlike other loadings, the nominal values for installation analysis including stiffness and

external forces must be best estimates rather than conservative values. Load factors should be applied for this case only at the member checking level and not at the level of the equilibrium analysis. The advantage of using LRFD rather than WSD is that the uncertainty is reflected for both the loading and strength rather by a single safety factor (strength) as with WSD. Thus, some situations or components which are more sensitive to the analysis variations would receive appropriate higher load factors in the safety checking. Members which may carry high loads but where the load effect is not likely to vary significantly should have lower load factors.

The techniques for deriving the load factors, for say the launch condition, are relatively straightforward as discussed in Section Comm. C.1. The steps in this instance would primarily include a careful sensitivity study of jacket reactions and member forces to different parameters (random variables) in the launch simulation, e.g., weight, buoyancy, drag force, inertia force, etc. This would provide sensitivity coefficients, $\Delta \mathbf{F}\mathbf{m} / \Delta \mathbf{X}\mathbf{i}$ , where: $\Delta \mathbf{F}\mathbf{m}$ are changes in member forces and $\Delta \mathbf{X}\mathbf{i} =$ unit change in random variable i. The respective member force coefficient of variation, VS, could be estimated as follows:

$$\begin{array}{r l} \text{V S} & = \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{s}}}{\overline{{\mathrm{S}}}} \end{array}$$

where:

$$\begin{array}{r l} \bar{\mathbf{S}} & = \text{n o m i n a l m e b e r} \\ & \text{p a r a m e t e r s , a n d} \end{array}$$

$$\sigma_{s} = \text{s t a n d a r d d e v i a t i o n o f f o r c e t o b e c a l c u l a t e d}$$

$$\sigma_{s}^{2} = \Sigma \left(\frac{\Delta F m}{\Delta X i}\right)^{2} \sigma X i^{2}$$

where

$$o \mathrm{X i} = \text{s t a n d a r d}$$

It will be difficult to precisely estimate $\sigma \mathbf{X}\mathbf{i}$ . One way is to try and estimate characteristic values, e.g., the chance that Xi will actually exceed some fractile, say 95th percentile. This leads to an approximate estimate for sigma using normal probability tables.

This approach, although not precise in a statistical sense, would provide sufficient parameters to do a subsequent calibration study, that is, review existing practices with known field performances and arrive at load factors which produce acceptable values of safety index, beta. One possibility is that there may already exist sensitivity studies which have accomplished these purposes.

Launch simulation is probably the most difficult of any installation phase for which to develop load factors, because of the nature of the analysis. Other aspects such as lift or transport should be more amendable to a load factor approach.

Load factors should not be confused with dynamic or impact factors. The latter are the increase in load effect due to inertia. Load factors account for the uncertainty in estimating the combined effect of static and dynamic loading. In fact, increases in static lift loads as recommended by RP2A WSD editions suggest that load factors for each phase of platform installation may be desirable. Reference C4 gives an example of load factors derived from some heavy lift operations. The advantage is the emphasis on uncertainties and the application of higher load factors to those elements sensitive to uncertain load fluctuations including static (due to tolerances) and dynamic conditions.

The cost issue can be quite different for different aspects of installation. For example, an increase in safety factor for a sling is going to be much less expensive than a similar increase for fatigue on a long tow. Such costs represent an important part of any installation provisions.

Comm. C.5.5 Lifting Forces. Lifting forces on padeyes and on other members of the structure should include both vertical and horizontal components, the latter occurring when lift slings are other than vertical. Vertical forces on the lift should include buoyancy as well as forces imposed by the lifting equipment. When suspended, the lift will occupy a position such that the center of gravity of the lift and the centroid of all upward acting forces on the lift are in static equilibrium. The position of the lift in this state of static equilibrium should be used to determine forces in the structure and in the slings. The movement of the lift as it is picked up and set down should be taken into account in determining critical combinations of vertical and horizontal forces at all points, including those to which lifting slings are attached. For lifts where either the lifting derrick or the structure to be lifted is on a floating vessel, the selection of the nominal lifting forces should consider the impact from vessel motion. The lift should be designed so that all structural steel members are proportioned for factored resistances as specified in Section B. In addition, all critical structural connections and primary members should be designed to have adequate reserve strength to ensure structural integrity during lifting.

Comm. C.5.8.1 Launched Structures. Guyed tower and template type structures that are transported by

barge are usually launched at or near the installation location. The jacket is generally moved along ways, which terminate in rocker arms, on the deck of the barge. As the position of the jacket reaches a point of unstable equilibrium, the jacket rotates, causing the rocker arms at the end of the ways to rotate as the jacket continues to slide from the rocker arms. Forces supporting the jacket on the ways should be evaluated for the full travel of the jacket. Deflection of the rocker beam and the effect on loads throughout the jacket should be considered. In general, the most severe forces will occur at the instant rotation starts.

Tower type structures are generally launched from the fabrication yard to float with their own buoyancy for tow to the installation site. The last portion of such a tower leaving the launching ways may have localized forces imposed on it as the first portion of the tower to enter the water gains buoyancy and causes the tower to rotate from the slope of the ways. Forces should be evaluated for the full travel of the tower down the ways.

COMM.C.6 ACCIDENTAL LOADS

Design consideration should be given to the potential for vessel collision and dropped objects. The severity and likelihood of these accidental events depend on many factors including operating environments, service vessel size, material handling equipment, and operator qualifications and proximity to shipping lanes. The collision and dropped object criteria should therefore depend on the platform location, operational procedures adopted and safety measures taken.

Collision and dropped object design criteria are difficult to quantify for three reasons: (1) the interaction of human and equipment error that combine to cause an accident is not quantifiable in probabilistic terms, (2) satisfaction of arbitrary quantification rules is no guarantee that safety will be achieved for any given accident and (3) satisfying simple rules will obviate the need to explore potentially inexpensive preventive measures.

Where consequences are very great and the probabilities of accidents occurring are very low, preventive measures may adequately serve to provide the necessary safety. For example, measures to prevent tanker collision are acceptable if they are effective; designing to resist a tanker collision is not a practical approach.

COMMENTARY D CYLINDRICAL MEMBER DESIGN

COMM.D.1GENERAL

This specification has been developed specifically for fabricated circular tubular shapes which are typical of offshore platform construction. Other structural shapes should be designed on the basis of the AISC-LRFD Specification, Reference D3. Load Factors for all platform components should be consistent with this API practice so that the entire platform can be analyzed as a single coherent model. Mixing API and AISC-LRFD factors would result in inconsistent safety indices. However, the nominal strength equations of the AISC-LRFD practice should be used to design noncylindrical shapes. This approach may appear inconsistent, since the API and AISC load factors are somewhat different. For a simple dead plus live load condition these factors can be compared as follows:

AISC 1.2(D) + 1.6(L)

API 1.3 (D) + 1.5 (L)

where: $\mathbf{D} =$ dead load

L = live load

Using the AISC target ratio of $\mathbf{L} / \mathbf{D} = 3.0$ , we can determine the weighted load factors as follows:

$$A I S C \quad \frac{(1 . 2) (1) + (1 . 6) (3)}{4} = 1. 50$$

$$\mathrm{A P I} \quad \frac{(1 . 3) (1) + (1 . 5) (3)}{4} = 1. 45$$

For this condition, the AISC weighted load factor is $3.4\%$ greater than that for API. However, the nontubular shapes that would utilize the AISC Specification are found primarily in deck superstructures where the dead load contribution is typically more significant than for any other part of the platform. As the dead load contribution increases and approaches a 1:1 ratio with the live load, the difference between the API and AISC weighted load factors become negligible. Therefore, using the API load factors with the AISC nominal strength equations and resistance factors for nontubular members in the deck superstructure should result in a reasonably consistent set of numerical values.

The required member strength specified in Section D has been expressed in the form of an inequality where the stress or force due to the factored loads must be less than or equal to the nominal strength times the associated resistance factor.

The resistance factors and nominal strength equations prescribed herein have been calibrated to produce consistent reliabilities under circumstances generally prevailing with RP2A - Working Stress Design (WSD) (Reference D4) using several Gulf of Mexico platforms. Appropriate resistance factors may need to be derived in cases where the structural components do not correspond to elements described herein or where additional input data become available from tests, measurements, etc. In such cases, a reliability analysis as outlined in

Comm. B may be used to develop the resistance factors. Such analyses should include uncertainty in material properties and deviations introduced by quality control procedures, variability in dimensions and fabrication and uncertainty in strength prediction models, including test scatter. Target reliabilities should be based on a reasonable likelihood of the failure consequences and compatibility with target reliabilities for other components that are covered in this practice.

Comm. D.1.1 Simplified Procedures. In lieu of performing a complete reliability analysis for those situations not covered by the factors contained herein, the following simplified procedures should produce acceptable reliability levels. A nominal strength formula shall be established by fitting test data combined with analytical verification. Scatter in strength prediction due to all causes shall be considered. A resistance coefficient of variation (COV), $\mathbf{V}_{\mathbb{R}}$ , should be estimated as follows:

$$\mathbf{V}_{\mathbf{R}} = \left(\mathbf{V}_{\mathbf{P}}^{2} + \mathbf{V}_{\mathbf{M}}^{2} + \mathbf{V}_{\mathbf{F}}^{2}\right)^{1 / 2} \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \tag{Comm.D-1}$$

where

$$\begin{array}{r l} \mathbf{V}_{\mathbf{P}} & = \mathbf{C}. \mathbf{O}. \mathbf{V}. \text{d u e t o t e s t o p r e d i c t e d d a t a s c a t t e r} \\ & \text{w i t h r e s p e c t t o m e a n v a l u e o f t e s t d a t a}, \end{array}$$

$$\begin{array}{r l} \mathbf{V}_{\mathbf{M}} & = \mathrm{C . O . V .} \text{d u e t o m a t e r i a l v a r i a b i l i t y r e p r e s e n t a t i v e f o u l - s c a l e m e m e b e r s n o t c o n s i d e d i n} \\ & \text{t e s t o p r e d i c t i o n d a t a , a n d} \end{array}$$

$$\begin{array}{r l} \mathbf{V}_{\mathrm{F}} & = \text{C . O . V . d u e t o f a b r i c a t i o n v a r i a b i l i t y r e p r e s e n t a t i v e o f f u l l - s c a l e m e b e r s w h i c h m a y} \\ & \text{n o t b e a c c o n t e d f o r i n t e s t o p r e d i c t i o n} \\ & \text{d a t a .} \end{array}$$

A calibration for the resistance factor, $\overline{\phi}$ , is shown in Table Comm. D.1-1 as a function of $\mathbf{V}_{\mathbb{R}}$ .

The values of $\overline{\phi}$ given are assumed to factor the mean strength. If the nominal strength is biased with respect to the mean strength, then the resistance factor can be revised as follows:

$$\phi = \bar{\phi} \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{R}} \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \tag{Comm.D-2}$$

where

$\overline{\phi}$ = resistance factor from Table Comm. D.1-1.

$\mathbf{B}_{\mathbb{R}} = \text{ratio of mean strength to nominal strength}$ ,

These resistance factors are to be used only in conjunction with the load factors prescribed herein.

Average target safety indices consistent with other design components are used in deriving these resistance factors. These indices may be reduced at the discretion of the operator if satisfactory field performance has been observed with the design procedure or if the consequences of component failure do not impair the overall safety of the platform structure.

COMM. D.2 CYLINDRICAL MEMBERS UNDER TENSION, COMPRESSION, BENDING, SHEAR, OR HYDROSTATIC PRESSURE

The compression, bending, and hydrostatic pressure recommendations contained in this section are based on a substantial program of testing carried out since 1975. Funding has been provided by the American Petroleum Institute, American Iron and Steel Institute, and by joint industry groups sponsored by offshore operators, contractors and consultants. All testing through 1985 has been documented in the references cited. Figures showing test results supporting the recommendations of Section D.2 are included in this commentary.

The design recommendations are tailored to cylinders of dimensions and material yield strengths typical of offshore platform members $\left(\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{y}} < 114 \mathrm{MPa}\right.$ (60 ksi) and $\mathrm{D} / \mathrm{t} < 120$ ). The local buckling formulas recommended for axial compression, bending and hydrostatic pressure are, however, considered valid up to $\mathrm{D} / \mathrm{t} < 300$ . Application of the recommendations to thin cylinders with high D/t ratios (>300) and high strength steels $\left[\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{y}} > 114 \mathrm{MPa}\right.$ (60 ksi)] may lead to unconservative results.

Comm. D.2.1 Axial Tension. The nominal strength equation for axial tension is applicable only for yielding of the gross section of circular cylinders. This condition should cover the large majority of tubular members in offshore platforms. For noncylindrical members, where the net section is less than the gross section or where fracture in the net section is a consideration, refer to the AISC-LRFD Specification for Steel Buildings, latest edition, Reference D3.

The resistance factor for axial tensile strength, $\phi_{\mathrm{t}} = 0.95$ , results in safety indices ( $\beta$ values) somewhat lower than those implied by the nominal strength equations

for other types of member behavior. However, the safety indices in tension still exceed those implied for extreme loading in the present API RP2A-WSD, Reference D4. The safety indices may also be lower than implied for other components since the consequences of tension yielding are less severe than other tubular member failure conditions, such as local buckling and general instability.

Comm. D.2.2 Axial Compression. Cylindrical members under axial compression are subject to failure due either to material yield, overall column buckling, or local buckling. Column buckling is discussed in Comm. D.2.2.1, and local buckling and material yield are discussed in Comm. D.2.2.2, below.

Comm. D.2.2.1 Column Buckling. The nominal strength equations for axial compression (Equations D.2.2-2a, D2.2-2b) are a function of the column slenderness parameter, $\lambda$ , which in turn is a function of the traditional slenderness ratio, KL/r. It can be shown that the nominal equation is the same as the API RP2A-WSD equation except for the safety factor. It is also identical to one of the column design equations recommended by the Structural Stability Research Council (SSRC) (Reference D5). The LRFD equation combined with a resistance factor （$\phi_{\mathrm{c}})$ of 0.85 yields safety indices of approximately 2.8 over a wide range of slenderness values （$\lambda)$ for W/G = 5, where W is the environmental load effect from wind, wave and current and G is the gravity load effect. The $\beta$ vs. $\lambda$ curves for different W/G ratios for the LRFD column equations are given in Reference D6.

The column buckling data base consists of ten fabricated pipe columns tested by Chen and Ross (Reference D7) and six pipe columns tested by Bouwkamp (Reference D8). Altogether these tests span the practical range of the column slenderness parameter （$\lambda)$ for offshore tubular members, and they are plotted in Figure Comm. D.2-1. References D7 and D8 give a thorough description of the specimens, instrumentation, test procedures and test results. The statistical treatment of these test data and an alternative mean strength equation are given in Reference D6.

The present API RP2A-WSD column design equations are based on the AISC WSD (Reference D9) and considered somewhat conservative. The AISC equations were based on compressive residual stresses that can develop in the heavy hot-rolled WF-shapes at the flange tips and at the flange-web intersections, which lead to somewhat different behavior than observed in fabricated cylinders.

The process of cold-rolling a flat plate into a circular cylinder does not typically induce as high a level of longitudinal compressive residual stresses as does the process of hot-rolling the heavier WF-shapes. This factor, in turn, appears to allow fabricated circular cylinders to achieve somewhat higher column strengths than the heavier, hot-rolled, WF-shapes. Equations D.2.2-2, with a resistance factor, $\phi_{\mathrm{c}}$ , of 0.85, result in acceptable $\beta$ values using the column buckling data base provided

FIG.COMM.D.2-1

COMPARISON OF TEST DATA WITH THE COLUMN BUCKLING

by the Chen and Ross and the Bouwkamp test programs cited above. The resistance factor of 0.85 is identical to that used in the AISC-LRFD practice. For shapes other than circular tubes, the AISC Load and Resistance Factor Design Specification for Steel Buildings, latest edition, (Reference D3) should be used.

Interaction between local and column buckling modes can occur, particularly if the critical load for local buckling is similar to the critical load for column buckling. Such interaction has been shown to be more pronounced with sections that are not torsionally stiff. Since cylindrical members are torsionally stiff, this interaction should be less of a problem than with many "open shapes" that have little torsional rigidity. Reference D5, Chapter 4, states that this conclusion is based on the small-deflection theory of plate buckling and the fact that, for most structural columns fabricated from plates or shapes, the lengths between nodes for column and local buckling are decidedly different. However, cylindrical column tests carried out at the University of Illinois in the 1930s for relatively high D/t ratios have indicated a noticeable interaction between local and column buckling. Because of such uncertainties, due to the significant loss of capacity that cylindrical shapes often incur with the onset of local buckling, and due to the fact that the interaction of buckling modes is complex and not fully understood, API has taken a conservative approach to such interaction in the past. This approach, as suggested by Marshall (Reference D10), involves substituting the local buckling strength for the yield strength, $\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{y}}$ , in the appropriate column formula. Pending a more definitive understanding of the interaction phenomenon in circular cylinders through further research, this API-LRFD practice will continue using the approach suggested by Marshall.

Comm. D.2.2.2 Local Buckling Short cylindrical members under axial compression will fail either by material yield or local buckling depending on the diameter-to-thickness （$\mathrm{D} / \mathrm{t})$ ratio. Cylindrical shells for low D/t ratios are generally not subject to local buckling under axial compression and can be designed on the basis of material failure, i.e., the local buckling stress may be considered equal to the yield stress. However, as the D/t ratio increases, the shell must be checked for local buckling.

Unstiffened thin-wall cylinders under axial compression and bending are prone to sudden failures at loads well below theoretical buckling loads predicted by classical small-deflection shell theory. There is a sudden drop in load-carrying capacity upon buckling. The post-buckling reserve strength of cylindrical members is small, in contrast to the post-buckling behavior of flat plates in compression, which continue to carry substantial load after buckling. For this reason, there is a need for more conservativeness in the definition of buckling load for cylinders than for most other structural elements. This is made difficult by the large scatter in test data, and necessitates a relatively conservative design procedure. The large scatter in test data is considered

to be the result of initial imperfections caused by fabrication tolerances and procedures. In addition to geometric imperfections, experimental and theoretical evidence has shown that the buckling load is also affected by boundary conditions and residual stresses built-in may hasten the buckling process.

Some recent experimental evidence indicates that inelastic local buckling may be less sensitive to initial imperfections and residual stresses than elastic local buckling (Reference D11).

The local buckling data base consists of about 52 tests performed by seven different investigators as described in Reference D6. The statistical treatment of these data that led to better understanding of nominal resistance and specification of resistance factor in Section D.2.2. The nominal strength equations are separated so that one applies in the elastic range Equation D.2.2-3 and the other applies in the inelastic range Equation D.2.2-4a, 4b. Cylindrical members used in offshore structures will normally fall into the inelastic range.

The test data and the nominal inelastic local buckling strength equation, Equations D.2.2-4a, -4b, are plotted in Figure Comm. D.2-2. This equation coupled with a resistance factor of 0.85 results in safety indices that meet or exceed the target value of 2.8 over the practical range of D/t ratios. Using the same resistance factor (0.85) for both the nominal local and column buckling equations allows one to substitute the local buckling strength into the column equation in order to capture the effect of interaction of the local and column buckling modes as described above.

The elastic local buckling stress formula recommended in Equation D.2.2-3 represents one-half the theoretical local buckling stress computed using classical small-deflection theory. This reduction accounts for the detrimental effect of geometric imperfections. Based on the test data shown in Figure Comm. D.2-2, it is considered to be conservative for cylinders with $t \geq 6$ mm ( $\frac{1}{4}$ in.) and $\mathrm{D} / \mathrm{t} < 300$ . Offshore platform members typically fall within these dimensional limits. For thinner cylinders and cylinders with higher $\mathrm{D} / \mathrm{t}$ ratios, larger imperfection reduction factors may be required.

The local buckling data base limits the applicability of the nominal strength equations to $\mathrm{D} / \mathrm{t} < 300$ and $\mathrm{t} \geq 6\mathrm{mm}$ (\% in.). API Bulletin 2U, Reference D1, provides guidance for the design of tubular members beyond these dimensional limits using an allowable stress design approach. The Bulletin 2U equations have not been statistically evaluated to find a corresponding resistance factor and safety index compatible with the LRFD approach. In lieu of such a statistical evaluation, a resistance factor of 0.85 may be used with the nominal equations given in API Bulletin 2U.

Comm. D.2.3 Bending. The ultimate bending moment capacity of fabricated circular cylinders, normalized with respect to yield moment capacity （$\mathbf{M}_{\mathrm{u}} / \mathbf{M}_{\mathrm{y}})$ is illustrated in Figure Comm. D.2-3. The data used in the

figure is from Sherman (Reference D12) and Stephens, et al. (Reference D13), and illustrate that at low $\mathbf{F_y}$ D/t ratios the ultimate moment capacities often substantially exceed the theoretical plastic moment capacities due to material strain hardening.

Although substantial scatter of the test data is observed, simply supported beam tests have smaller moment capacities than the fixed end beam tests. Similarly, a reduction in moment capacity is observed with the reduction in support rigidity. However, the end condition has little influence on the rotational capacity of the cylinder. At low $\mathbf{F}_{\mathbf{y}}$ D/t the plastic hinge mechanism forms over a short length of the cylinder. As the end support rigidity is reduced, the hinge mechanism forms over a longer segment of the cylinder. As $\mathbf{F}_{\mathbf{y}}$ D/t for the cylindrical shell increase, both the moment and rotational capacities decrease.

To define the behavior of a cylindrical shell accurately, the behavior of the cylinder subjected to bending is grouped into three regions:

I) High rotational capacity - ductile failure mode, exhibiting very gradual load decay.   
II) Intermediate rotational capacity - semiductile failure mode, exhibiting still gradual load decay.   
III) Low rotational capacity - little post-yield ductility, exhibiting susceptibility to local buckling and rapid load decay.

The recommended formulations defining the nominal bending strengths were calibrated to develop ultimate

moment capacities that reflect the test results. Since the strain hardening varies from one steel to another, the formulations defined are also restricted so that the ultimate moment capacities do not exceed theoretical plastic moment capacities. Thus, Region I, extending up to $\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{y}}$ D/t equal to 10,340 MPa (1500 ksi) allows for development of the full plastic moment capacity. The full plastic moment capacity is linearly reduced to $10\%$ in excess of the yield moment capacity (i.e., $\mathbf{M_u} / \mathbf{M_y} = 1.10$ ) at $\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{y}}$ D/t equal to 20,680 MPa (3000 ksi), representing a transition between Regions I and III. Since very few data points are available in Region III, the recommended formulation defining this region is intentionally made somewhat conservative.

The experimental results, particularly those in Region III, indicate local buckling mode shapes on the compressive side of the specimens similar to those indicated in equivalent specimens tested under axial compressive loads. However, the extreme fiber bending stresses under the failure bending moments are significantly higher than the local buckling stresses for the equivalent specimens under axial compressive loads in the practical ranges of D/t ratios commonly found in typical offshore structures. These characteristics are reflected in Figure Comm. D.2-3. The failure bending stresses approach the local buckling stresses at large D/t ratios such as 300, when the stresses are elastic. It is logical to anticipate that the buckling mode shapes for such large D/t ratios are likely to be of multiple wave length, such that the extreme fiber stresses due to bending moments over a one-half wave length are similar to those due to axial compressive loads.

![](API_RP_2A-LRFD_1st/chunk2_aaef82d460f7f8679a7c9c44762c97f2f834e5729a4f3667d963e296b33527fb.jpg)  
FIG.COMM.D.2-3 COMPARISON OF TEST DATA WITH BENDING DESIGN EQUATION FOR FABRICATED CYLINDERS SUBJECTED TO BENDING

The API RP2A working stress design (WSD) (Reference D4) and the present LRFD formulations are both based on the same relationship defining ultimate moment capacity normalized with respect to yield moment capacity （$\mathbf{M}_{\mathrm{u}} / \mathbf{M}_{\mathrm{y}})$ . The LRFD nominal bending stress formulation defines the full plastic capacity of a cylindrical section in Region I, while the WSD formulation for allowable bending stress multiplied by the safety factor (1.67) yields slightly less than the full plastic capacity (27.3% above yield vs. 25% above yield).

The nominal bending stress formulations coupled with a resistance factor, $\phi_{\mathrm{b}}$ , result in relatively uniform implied safety indices. A $\phi_{\mathrm{b}}$ of 0.95 will provide satisfactory target indices exceeding 2.7 over the practical range of $\mathbf{F}_{\mathbf{y}}\mathbf{D} / \mathbf{t}$ .

The utilization of bending stress formulations instead of bending moment formulations such as those in the AISC LRFD Specifications (Reference D3) is intended to maintain the merits of the traditional system, such as the AISC Specifications (Working Stress Method, Reference D9). The stress formulations and the resulting design stresses provide more informative values to designers in their evaluation and design processes than the member loads such as bending moments or axial loads. The upper limits of member ultimate stresses in most failure modes are well understood to be the yielding of the material. The reserves in a specific member can be appreciated in an approximate manner in terms of member stress and the yield strength, although a more thorough examination of elastic buckling and inelastic yielding strengths are required for a design decision. The appreciation of the approximate reserves by assessing member stresses provides designers an advantage by which, together with interaction ratios, they can evaluate both elastic buckling and inelastic yielding conditions. The member load formulations provide designers the information regarding the reserves against the lower of the above two strength parameters, but, in most cases, the designers would have no knowledge of how close the member loads are to yielding the material.

Since the LRFD nominal bending strength exceeds the elastic yield moment for low D/t ratios, the bending stress, as calculated by M/S, is in fact an equivalent elastic bending stress, when M exceeds $\mathbf{M_y}$ . The equivalent elastic bending stress does not reflect the actual bending stress distribution across the cross section under this condition. However, it provides a convenient term for design purposes. Other alternatives, such as a coefficient to indicate mobilization of the inelastic portion of the bending strength may be introduced to supplement the traditional design parameters.

Comm. D.2.5 Hydrostatic Pressure

Comm. D.2.5.1 Design Hydrostatic Head. The load factors for determining the hydrostatic pressure to use in checking the adequacy of the design are 1) 1.3 for the functional load case (e.g., pressures that will definitely be encountered during the installation or life of

the structure) and 2) 1.1 for the case where interaction with storm loads is considered.

Comm. D.2.5.2 Hoop Buckling. The introduction of LRFD provided an opportunity to review hydrostatic buckling test data used to develop provisions in RP2A-WSD. In addition, recent test programs sponsored by API and others have provided more test data relevant to platform tubulars. Test results are reported (References D14-17) cover the range of D/t, L/D, and $\mathbf{F_y}$ applicable to the cylindrical members of typical fixed platforms.

Since hydrostatic buckling is a potentially severe failure mode, safety indices were set at the upper end of the range determined from calibration with WSD, namely, above 3.0 for the functional load case. A careful review of the scatter, namely, that from tests (9.5-11.3%), fabrication (5%), elastic modulus (6%), and material (8%) yielded values of overall COV of 10-15%, depending on the value of $\mathbf{F_{he}} / \mathbf{F_y}$ . A bias due to material yield and test was also present. This information is described in detail in the final report of PRAC 85-22. Together, these data and an assumed load COV of 5% produced that exceeded the target value for the full range of $\mathbf{F_{he}} / \mathbf{F_y}$ .

A similar evaluation for WSD, using the equations in RP2A-WSD for strength with the associated safety factors, produced much higher safety margins even including the one-third increase in allowable. The main reason is that the checking equations in RP2A-WSD are based on conservative lower bound to the available test data (which did not include some of the recent test data).

The form of the relationship for the critical hoop buckling stress, $\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{hc}}$ in Equation D.2.5-2 is similar to that in RP2A-WSD. That is, $\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{hc}}$ is dependent on the elastic hoop buckling stress, $\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{he}}$ , which is a function of the geometrical parameters, D/t and M.

Equation D.2.5-4b is a "mean" equation and was formulated by regression analysis to fit the test data. Note that Equation D.2.5-4a is compatible with the equations given in the final report of PRAC 86-55 (Reference D6), but rewritten into RP2A-WSD format. Figure Comm. D.2-4 shows the comparison for the ultimate and allowable strengths between the recommended and RP2A-WSD equations.

The reformatted equations for $C_h$ given in the final report of PRAC 86-55 give very similar $C_h$ values when compared with those equations in RP2A-WSD. Hence, the RP2A-WSD equations defining $C_h$ are adopted here because of a familiarity of designers to the equations.

Comm. D.2.5.3 Ring Stiffener Design. The formula given for determining the moment of inertia of stiffening rings, Equation D.2.5-6, provides sufficient strength to resist buckling of the ring and shell even after the shell has buckled between stiffeners. It is assumed that the shell offers no support after buckling and transfers all its load to the effective stiffener section. The stif

fener ring is designed as an isolated ring that buckles into two waves （$n = 2)$ at a collapse pressure 20 percent higher than the strength of the shell.

Comm. D.2.5.4 Geometric Imperfections. Equation D.2.5-5 for determining the elastic hoop buckling strength, $\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{he}}$ , of the cylindrical member represents 80% of the theoretical hoop buckling strength obtained using small-deflection classical theory. The implied 20% reduction accounts for the effect of geometric imperfections due to fabrication. All of the available data indicate that the reduction is reasonably conservative for cylinders fabricated within the API Spec 2B out-of-roundness tolerances, Reference D2.

For cylinders with out-of-roundness values greater than the maximum allowable in API Spec 2B less than $3\%$ , the elastic hoop buckling test results suggest that it is necessary to reduce $\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{he}}$ , as defined in Equation D.2.5-5. One method for the reduction of $\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{he}}$ is given by:

Reduced

$$\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{h e}} = \alpha \mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{h e}} / 0. 8 \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \tag{Comm.D.2.5-1a}$$

in which geometric imperfection factor $\alpha$ is given by:

$$\alpha = 1. 0 - 0. 2 \sqrt{\frac{D_{\max} - D_{\min}}{0 . 01 D_{\mathrm{n o m}}}} \dots \dots \text{C o m m . D}. 2. 5 - 1 b$$

where

$$\frac{\mathrm{D}_{\max } - \mathrm{D}_{\min }}{0 . 01 \mathrm{D}_{\text{n o m}}} = \text{o u t - o f - r o u n d n e s s (e)}$$

Figure Comm. D.2-4 shows the comparison for the ultimate strength between the LRFD and RP2A-WSD equations. The test data plotted in the figure are those reported in Reference D6. The reduction of $\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{he}}$ given by Equation Comm. D.2.5-1 was not carried out in plotting the test data on Figure Comm. D.2-4. The test data would shift slightly to the right if the reduction has been made. However, this shift in the test data will have negligible impact on Equations D.2.5-4 for the critical hoop buckling strength, $\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{hc}}$ .

COMM. D.3 CYLINDRICAL MEMBERS UNDER COMBINED LOADS. This section of the commentary describes the background of the design recommendation

![](API_RP_2A-LRFD_1st/chunk2_4f6cba8c977467d8c6bdb51444c886d1dfa0266eded86ef1ea26623af26cdfb8.jpg)  
FIG.COMM.D.2-4 COMPARISON OF TEST DATA WITH HOOP BUCKLING DESIGN EQUATIONS FOR FABRICATED CYLINDERS UNDER HYDROSTATIC COMPRESSION

tions in Section D.3, which covers unstiffened and ringstiffened cylindrical shell instability mode interactions when subjected to combined axial, bending, and external pressure loads. While Sections D.3.1 and D.3.2 discuss global interaction of axial and bending loads, Sections D.3.3 and D.3.4 cover local interaction of axial, bending and hydrostatic external pressure loads.

Due to limited test data on high external pressure loads, there are uncertainties on local and global interaction. Thus, possible degradation of member axial load carrying capacity due to high external pressures cannot be defined. Considering the design and installation of platforms in deep water.

Comm. D.3.1 Combined Axial Tension and Bending. This section provides a strength check for components under combined axial tensile load and bending. The interaction equation is of the "cosine form" which is similar for the axial compression and bending case except that $\phi_{\mathrm{t}}$ is used with the axial tension case instead of $\phi_{\mathrm{c}}$ with the axial compression case. Note that if the bending stress is larger than the axial tensile stress, then the local buckling effect due to bending (compression side) should be properly considered in the bending strength （$\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{bn}})$ in Equation D.3.1-1.

Due to the cosine term, be sure to use the largest interaction ratio from Equations D.2.1-1 and D.3.1-1.

Comm. D.3.2 Combined Axial Compression and Bending. This section provides an overall beam-column stability check, Equation D.3.2-1, and strength check, Equation D.3.2-2, for components under combined axial load and bending.

Equation D.3.2-1 maintains the present AISC-WSD beam column stability interaction equation (Reference D9). This equation is conservative with respect to small scale tubular member tests and analyses of larger sections performed with assumed imperfections and residual stresses. As data accumulates on this subject, a reliability calibration of the form of this interaction may be appropriate.

Equation D.3.2-2, the interaction equation for a strength check, is of the "cosine form" which fits this type of phenomenon and exists in RP2A-WSD (Reference D4) in both the overload check on piles and the interaction equation for tubular connections. Equation D.3.2-2 is identically equivalent to an "arc sine" form but is preferred to avoid computer errors when the argument of the arc sine exceeds 1.0. It should be noted in comparison that the cosine form (or arc sine) may be up to $10\%$ less conservative than the linear interaction form. Thus, comparisons of members with significant bending and axial contributions may show lower interaction ratios. This is a consequence of the more accurate interaction equation rather than the load or resistance factors themselves. The influence of $\mathrm{D} / \mathrm{t}$ on the strength interaction equation is contained in both $\mathbf{F}_{\mathbf{x}\mathbf{c}}$ ,in Equation

D.2.2-4b and $\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{bn}}$ , which contains D/t in Equation D.2.3-2a, -2b, and -2c.

Equation D.3.2-2 should be used for the design of pile segments below the mudline. However, for the analysis of laterally loaded piles, with significant axial loads, the secondary moments or $\mathbf{P} - \Delta$ effects should be considered in the stress computations for $\mathbf{f}_{\mathrm{by}}$ and $\mathbf{f}_{\mathrm{bz}}$ in Equation D.3.2-2.

The recommendations for the slenderness ratio, $\mathrm{Kl} / \mathbf{r}$ and the reduction factor $C_{\mathrm{m}}$ for tubular members under axial compressive loads are identical to existing RP2A-WSD provisions. Since the slenderness ratio is usually found to be conservative using existing provisions, when a more accurate analysis is used to calculate member effective lengths, consideration should be given to reducing the compression resistance factor $\phi_{\mathrm{c}}$ especially in the range of $\lambda$ above 1.0.

Comm. D.3.3 Combined Axial Tension, Bending and Hydrostatic Pressure. For members with the critical hoop buckling stress, $\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{hc}}$ , approaching the yield stress, $\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{y}}$ , Equation D.3.3-1 reduces to the Beltrami-Haigh yield equation for biaxial stress condition, which is based on the maximum strain energy theory. The form of the Beltrami-Haigh equation was first adopted in the 12th edition of RP2A (1981) with $\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{hc}}$ replacing $\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{y}}$ in the hoop compression term to account for interaction between hoop buckling and axial tension. The modified Beltrami-Haigh equation was found to agree reasonably well with all of the available test data at that time, which were for small diameter and low D/t ratios.

In 1980 and 1981, an extensive test program on large diameter, fabricated tubular members was conducted to generate test data for the verification of the modified Beltrami-Haigh equation. The test data are well documented in Reference D15. References D15 and D21 concluded that the modified Beltrami-Haigh equation is also reasonably conservative with respect to the fabricated tubular test data and its use was maintained in the RP2A, Reference D4.

For the elastic condition, it has been theoretically shown in Reference D22 that axial tension has no effect on the hoop buckling strength. That is, there is no interaction between axial tension and hoop compression for pure elastic behavior. However, the modified Beltrami-Haigh equation predicts interaction even at elastic conditions. So, further modifications to the modified Beltrami-Haigh equation were developed to remove this unnecessary conservatism by introducing the $\eta$ factor in Equation D.3.3-1. The use of the $\eta$ factor results in a family of interaction curves representing different ultimate behavior of members with different failure-yield stress ratios. The predicted ultimate behavior agrees with test data for fabricated tubular members, as discussed below, and also for casing members (Reference D23).

Figures Comm. D.3-1a and Comm. D.3-1b compare Equation D.3.3-1 with those in RP2A-WSD (Reference D4) and API BUL 2U (Reference D1), respectively. Safety and resistance factors have been excluded. Note that the ordinate is in terms of $\mathbf{f_h} / \mathbf{F_y}$ instead of $\mathbf{f_h} / \mathbf{F_{hc}}$ . Elastic hoop buckling is predicted when $\mathbf{f_h} / \mathbf{F_y} \leq 0.55$ , as stipulated in Equation D.2.5-4b. For zero net axial tension, all three equations give the same critical hoop buckling stress. For nonzero tension, Equation D.3.3-1 is generally less conservative than both RP2A-WSD and BUL 2U to describe the outer yield envelope. For the elastic condition, Equation D.3.3-1 agrees with the classical theory in that there is no axial tension-hoop compression interaction. Note that for tension greater than the proportional limit, but less than the yield stress, the elastic condition is no longer satisfied and interaction should be predicted.

Figures Comm. D.3-2a through Comm. D.3-2i illustrate the comparison of Equation D.3.3-1 with the fabricated test data reported in Reference D15. In normalizing the test ultimate loads, the measured static longitudinal and hoop tensile yield stresses were used; Reference D15 used the dynamic values. In plotting the predicted curve (solid line), the average value of the $\mathbf{F_{hc}} / \mathbf{F_y}$ ratios for each test group was used, and $\mathbf{F_{hc}}$ was calculated using measured dimensions, static $\mathbf{F_y}$ , and Equation D.2.5-4. The out-of-roundness correction, as specified in Comm. D.2.5 for specimens that have out-of-roundness greater than the maximum API allowable of $1\%$ , was used in determining $\mathbf{F_{hc}}$ . For all predicted curves, the resistance factors, $\phi_h$ and $\phi_t$ , have been omitted because there is no uncertainty in material and geometric properties for the test specimens.

In Figure Comm. D.3-2b, test 2E has higher test ultimate strength than the other tests in this group. The measured yield stresses for this group were similar. However, the out-of-roundness for specimen E was much smaller than those of the other specimens, which were greater than the maximum API allowable of $1\%$ Reference D2. The predicted curve for test 2E will be higher than the average curve shown in Figure Comm. D.3-2b since $\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{hc}}$ will be higher due to lower or no correction for out-of-roundness effect. Similar results are observed in Figures Comm. D.3-2c and -2d for test groups 3 and 4.

At first glance, it may appear that the predicted critical hoop buckling strength, $\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{hc}}$ (zero axial tension), is quite conservative for elastic hoop buckling condition (Figures Comm. D.3-2e and -2i). However, the predicted curve will agree with the data if the ordinate, $\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{hc}}$ , is accurately predicted. The conservatism can be traced to the length and D/t effects. It is not now clear how Equation D.2.5.5 (elastic hoop buckling strength) could be revised to account for more precise effect of length and D/t such that uniform reliability is realized

for the whole range of D/t ratio up to 300. More data are required.

All of the test data in Figures Comm. D.3-2 were from specimens loaded by combined axial tension and hoop compression with no bending moment. For design, the resultant bending stress acting on a member is taken as an equivalent tensile stress. This is a conservative approach, especially for small to moderate D/t ratios. Note that at the limit when there is no axial tension or external pressure, the predicted allowable bending stress is $\phi_{\mathrm{t}}\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{y}}$ instead of $\phi_{\mathrm{b}}\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{bn}}$ . For members subject to very high bending, other approaches (finite element analysis, pertinent test data, etc.) may be used to eliminate the unnecessary conservatism.

Comm. D.3.4 Combined Axial Compression, Bending and Hydrostatic Pressure. As stated in the introduction to Section D.3 of this commentary, the interaction relationship among axial compression, bending, and hydrostatic pressure is local. The combination of hydrostatic pressure and axial load may produce a different critical buckling stress than either of these load systems acting independently. In checking the member for column buckling and hydrostatic pressure by Equation D.3.2-1, the hydrostatic pressure contribution to axial stress is omitted simply to recognize that capped end tubular columns under hydrostatic pressure do not fail in a column buckling mode. Figure Comm. D.3-3 illustrates the recommended interaction equations for various possible stress conditions. These interaction equations imply that no interaction occurs if the axial stress is less than one-half the allowable hoop stress.

The recommended interaction equations have been checked against the results of available tests and found to give conservative results, as shown in Figures Comm. D.3-4, D.3-5 and D.3-6. Figure Comm. D.3-4 shows the results of elastic buckling tests on mylar, plexiglass, and fabricated steel cylinders, while Figure Comm. D.3-5 shows the results of fabricated steel cylinders alone. In Figure Comm. D.3-5 the test results are compared with the recommended equation for elastic interaction, Equation D.3.4-1, using $\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{xe}}$ and $\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{he}}$ values determined from the tests. This comparison validates the form of Equation D.3.4-1. In Figure Comm. D.3-5 the fabricated steel cylinder test results are compared with Equation D.3.4-1, using $\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{xe}}$ and $\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{he}}$ values computed from the design equations in Section D.2. This confirms that Equation D.3.4-1 is conservative. In Figure Comm. D.3-6, the recommended interaction equations are compared with the results of test data for unstiffened steel pipe with an elastic hydrostatic buckling stress and an inelastic axial buckling stress. This comparison demonstrates the validity of the recommended interaction equations for combined elastic and inelastic behavior.
