COMMENTARY E CONNECTIONS

COMM. E.1 CONNECTIONS OF TENSION AND COMPRESSION MEMBERS

The $50\%$ minimum capacity provision stems from the long-standing AISC requirement that was instituted for truss designs, Reference E2. The requirement originated in an age when fewer load cases were considered in the design stage and design tools were less sophisticated and thorough. Nevertheless, a minimum capacity provision is considered appropriate for contemporary offshore platforms in order to provide a safety net for collisions, dropped objects, and other unanticipated loads. The provision also ensures a minimum standard for connections of particular secondary members that take on primary importance in reserve strength assessments. However, the designer may judge the $50\%$ rule to be inappropriate in certain instances, such as the connections of some appurtenances.

The provision intends that the joint load from $50\%$ of the member strength (without safety factor) be compared to the ultimate joint capacity (also without safety factor). Hence, joints are made at least half as safe as the attached members. This requirement is in sharp contrast to the earthquake provision (C.4.4.1) in which the joints are required to have ultimate strength equal to $100\%$ of the member's effective strength.

Equation E.3-1 is introduced in order to simplify the minimum capacity check as well as reduce its dominance (Reference E3) for simple tubular joint designs. While the brace yield strength appears in the equation, the constants assume an average effective strength of $0.9\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{yb}}$ , meaning a compromise between tension and compression cases. The constants also assume that the brace stress is $75\%$ axial, $19\%$ in-plane bending, and $6\%$ out-of-plane bending. Finally, the derivation includes a weighting of joint classifications between K, T/Y, and X.

The requirement of Equation E.3-1 has been compared to joint designs for the normal suite of loading conditions on four different platforms. For 107 joints where dominance of Equation E.3-1 was not considered appropriate, the average unity check for Equation E.3-1 was about 83 percent of the unity check for normal loads. This figure implies a lesser joint "can" thickness for the minimum capacity requirement, as expected.

COMM. E.3 TUBULAR JOINTS

Simple Joints. Early design requirements for the static strength of simple tubular joints were stated in terms of nominal punching shear stress (Reference E4). The 1973 version of RP2A (4th Edition) gave the punching shear capacity as:

$$\mathbf{v}_{\mathbf{p}} = \mathbf{Q}_{\beta} \mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{f}} \frac{\mathbf{F}_{\mathbf{y}}}{0 . 9 \gamma^{0 . 7}} \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \tag{Comm.E.3-1}$$

A later Welding Research Council comparison of the 1973 expression against an expanded data base prompted a major revision which first appeared in the 1977 version of RP2A (9th Edition):

$$\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{p}} = \mathbf{Q}_{\mathrm{q}} \mathbf{Q}_{\mathrm{p}} \mathbf{Q}_{\mathrm{f}} \frac{\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{y}}}{0 . 9 \gamma^{0 . 7}} \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \tag{Comm.E.3-2}$$

The $\mathbf{Q}_{\beta}$ factor had thereby evolved into a $\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{q}}$ table in order to differentiate among the performances of K joints (better), cross joints (worse, particularly at low $\beta$ ), and T joints (which dominated the original data base) (References E5, E6). Also, a $\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{p}}$ term was included to account for nonlinear interaction between brace axial and bending stress effects. The $\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{p}}$ expression was derived from plastic interaction of a tubular cross section, although its use was considered conservative relative to the analytical work in Reference E7.

The 1977 provisions remained virtually intact until the revisions to the 13th Edition (1982) were issued in 1983. New test data were available on load interaction effects on joint performance (Reference E8). Careful analysis of the background of Reference E8 revealed that its recommended linear interaction was misleading in that the data did not reflect inelastic behavior, as do the capacity data for individual brace loads. However, Figure Comm. E.3-1 shows that even with the data replotted, the $\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{p}}$ and $\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{q}}$ interpolation technique in RP2A was unconservative; separate interpolation of $\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{p}}$ and $\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{q}}$ for axial bending stresses led to an unanticipated synergism in the combined effect. As a temporary measure, it was decided to adopt the arcsin interaction rule which applies to tubular cross sections, appears elsewhere in RP2A, and was the original intent of the $\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{p}}$ expression.

While punching shear continues to be a useful concept, it rarely reflects the actual mode of failure at a joint. Localized stresses which limit the joint capacity are complex, involving variable shell bending and membrane stresses in addition to shear stress. The 15th Edition of RP2A addressed the shortcomings of the punching shear idea and included dramatic changes in the design criteria. These changes were based upon the work of Yura, et al., who performed additional large scale tests and screened the worldwide data base from which lower bound strength equations were developed (Reference E9). Unlike contemporary European practice, the equations were not rigorously established via statistical techniques, because in most instances, the data base was neither large enough to reliably represent a given joint type load condition nor indictive of the distribution of geometries found on real platforms. Also contrary to European practice, displacement and first crack failure limits were considered in addition to peak loads achieved in the test. This displacement condition should not be confused with a serviceability

![](API_RP_2A-LRFD_1st/chunk2_10cee4e680435c26d7676e6387283058d29f3d60a834b7feeb2761f16dffd57c.jpg)  
FIG.COMM.E.3-1 BRACE LOAD INTERACTION EQUATIONS

limit. A governing displacement limit in the Yura context implies that the peak load capacity in the test would never be achieved in the actual structure during a sequence of events required for collapse.

The most salient feature of the Yura results was the expression of joint strength in terms of brace nominal load instead of punching shear stress. However, essentially equivalent criteria can be formulated in both formats. Because member checks are entirely in the form of strength criteria, the LRFD RP2A presents only the nominal load expressions and not the essentially equivalent punching stress form.

The equations incorporated in the 15th Edition of RP2A (Note that 14th Edition was withdrawn) differed from those proposed by Yura in only one aspect. The gap factor, $\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{g}}$ , for K joints was adjusted to ensure a lower bound was achieved. Figure Comm. E.3-2 shows a plot of the K data with the revised gap parameter expressions. With gap expressed in this manner, $\gamma$ has little additional effect on capacity.

The 15th Edition of RP2A also included an important change in the capacity factor, $\mathbf{Q}_{\mathrm{f}}$ , for the interactive effect of chord loads. Figure Comm. E.3-3 suggests that the historic $\mathbf{Q}_{\mathrm{f}}$ expression was unconservative for most $\gamma$ values encountered on steel jackets (Reference E10). The new $\mathbf{Q}_{\mathrm{f}}$ expression also reflected a reduced importance of chord bending stress relative to chord axial stress. The A term in LRFD is now an average of the factored stress at opposite sides of the chord (a sort of vector

![](API_RP_2A-LRFD_1st/chunk2_74c3d1866b5667dea466591d082cfc7beea71e939ae2111e5a4bfeaa87dccc70.jpg)  
FIG.COMM.E.3-2 VARIATION OF K JOINT AXIAL LOAD CAPACITY WITH CHORD FLEXIBILITY

sum), not a straight summation. The yield stress resistance factor in the denominator of A is maintained, implying that chord and branch loads may all increase by this factor beyond design levels before failure of the joint is reached. Using factored stresses in the numerator and a resistance factor in the denominator will produce similar $\mathbf{Q}_{\mathrm{f}}$ values for LRFD and WSD.

The 15th Edition of RP2A made a slight modification in joint safety factor from 1.8 to 1.7. This change was primarily justified on the basis of the average joint design by the 15th Edition being thereby closer to the average joint design by the 13th Edition Supplement.

The LRFD provisions maintain the identical nominal strength equations (Yura) introduced into the 13th Edi

tion Supplement. The resistance factors for connections were confirmed by two types of studies. One study was a direct comparison of interaction ratios between LRFD and the 15th Edition (Yura); and the second study compared the safety indices obtained with punching stress (13th Edition), Yura (15th Edition) and LRFD. There are several reasons for not relying solely on safety indices for calibrating connection resistance factors and achieving a common beta in this edition for all connections. (a) The Yura equations have not yet been proved by field performance history. Such performance is the basis for calibrating other member performance in LRFD. (b) There is a possibility as expressed in the 15th Edition Commentary that the Yura equations are still too conservative, even after reduction of safety fac

![](API_RP_2A-LRFD_1st/chunk2_5f449cf0dfe90538fddf722fd3b6cbd828e191b9ff400cbdd3c1562576990e0f.jpg)  
FIG.COMM.E.3-3 CHORD STRESS REDUCTION EFFECTS FOR ALL BRANCH LOAD TYPES WITH SAFETY FACTOR REMOVED

tors from 1.8 to 1.7, and further reductions are possible. (c) Some of the test scatter in the Yura formulation is due to interpretations of failure in the test results rather than a true representation of uncertainty in ultimate strengths.

For the present calibration, betas were obtained for the 13th Edition (punching stress - WSD), 15th Edition (Yura - WSD), and LRFD (Yura). The data for the 13th Edition has a bias and coefficient of variation of 1.02 (17%), 1.08 (41%), 1.33 (27%), 1.79 (14%), and 1.71 (21%) for T, Y, and X compression, T, Y, X tension, K joint, in-plane bending, and out-of-plane bending, respectively. These data are taken directly from Reference E9, except that it also includes an additional bias of 1.10 and COV of 8% to reflect material yield stress variability. The data for the Yura strength formula (WSD or LRFD) has bias and COV values of 1.17 (11%), 1.55 (43%), 1.28 (19%), 1.35 (16%), and 1.29 (17%) for the same five connection categories. Except for the T, Y, X tension condition, the Yura equations have a lower COV than the punching shear indicating a better fit of the strength formula to test scatter. The exception for T, Y, X tension case, (43% - COV) is likely due to the definition of failure as first crack formation, which is hard to estimate in a test, and is probably not indicative of true ultimate strength variability. The average safety indices, ( $\beta$ ), for the three design formulas are:

AVERAGE BETA   



|  | T,Y,X | T,Y,X | T,Y,X | T,Y,X | T,Y,X |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | Compressiion | T,Y,X Tension | K Joints | In- Plane Bending | Out-of- Plane Bending |
| WSD-13th Edition | 1.90 | 1.31 | 2.26 | 3.61 | 3.17 |
| Yura-15th Edition | 2.33 | 1.85 | 2.30 | 2.59 | 2.40 |
| LRFD | 2.57 | 2.11 | 2.51 | 2.81 | 2.61 |



It can be seen that the spread in beta in the 13th Edition from 1.31 to 3.61 is very large and not conducive to consistent reliability-based design. The 15th Edition and LRFD are much more uniform and also close to each other. The LRFD average betas are similar for each joint type except for the tension case due to reasons cited above. Otherwise, the average betas are in the 2.50 - 2.80 range, typical of other steel component betas. Also, it is pointed out in the PRAC references that the spread in beta for each connection type with different environmental-to-gravity load ratios is smaller for LRFD than for the 15th Edition betas.

The resistance factor, $\phi_{\mathrm{j}}$ , chosen for LRFD to achieve the betas shown above was set as 0.90 for T, Y and cross joints in tension and 0.95 for all other cases. As more data accumulates from ongoing test programs, it is expected there will be further refinements of the resistance factors to produce even more consistent safety

indices among the various connection types. These safety indices may also be adjusted relative to member safety indices to achieve a proper balance between other steel components and their connections. These considerations involve economic and system aspects of reliability.

The resistance factors presented herein were also compared directly with the WSD format. Noting that the nominal strength equations are identical in the 15th Edition RP2A and the present RP2A-LRFD permits an easy comparison of interaction ratios for both formats. The basis for comparison is the ratio, R, of interaction ratios, I.R., for each format:

$$R = \frac{I . R . (L R F D)}{I . R . (W S D)} \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \tag{Comm.E.3-3}$$

Values of R above one indicate LRFD is more conservative, while values less than one mean the 15th Edition is more conservative. The maximum value is $\mathbf{R} = 1.18$ for an environmental condition with a 1.35 load factor and a 0.9 resistance factor for LRFD, compared to a safety factor of $1.7 \times \%$ for WSD. The smallest value of R is $\mathbf{R} = 0.80$ for a dead load case with a 1.30 load factor and 0.95 resistance factor compared to a safety factor of 1.7 for WSD. Thus, in comparing LRFD connection design with the 15th Edition, the maximum differences in interaction ratio will amount to about $\pm 20\%$ . This range of difference between LRFD and the 15th Edition was also borne out in the comparisons of joint checks for platforms A, B, and C. Scatter diagram plots of I.R. for LRFD vs. I.R. for 15th Edition, as well as tables comparing individual joints, showed considerable consistency among these checks, and the ratios generally fell in the $\pm 20\%$ range. Some exceptions occur due to the same reason cited in Section D in comparison of member interaction ratios. The differences in I.R. between either LRFD or 15th Edition compared with earlier RP2A editions were much greater because of the changes in nominal strength equation that occurred from the 13th to the 15th Edition. This was borne out in the scatter plots of I.R. produced for platforms A, B, and C using these three checking equations. Also, tables of comparison of individual joints showed ratios of I.R. values for LRFD (and 15th Edition) compared to 13th Edition ranging from 0.50 to 1.70.

Joint Classification. API has long recognized that joint classification should be based on load pattern as well as geometry. Classification is relevant to both fatigue and strength considerations. With regard to strength, the favorable $\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{u}} / \mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{q}}$ values for K-connections reflect their reduced joint can ovalizing as compared to T&Y-connections and the adverse $\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{u}} / \mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{q}}$ values for cross connections reflect their more severe ovalizing tendencies.

Several schemes for automating the classification process have evolved over the years. In all of them, member ends belonging to a particular node are identified, along with their geometry information (e.g., direction

cosines) and their loads for each design case. Member ends lying in a common plane, and on the same side of the chord as in a K-connection, are identified and the gaps between them are computed. Load pattern and member classification may change from one design case to the next. Each member end is examined for each load case, and different member end joint classifications may co-exist in the same node.

The logic of one scheme closely follows the examples of Figure E.3-2. Members whose punching load (component normal to the chord surface) is essentially balanced by loads in other members in the same plane, on the same side of the chord, are treated as K-connections, as in examples (a), (d), (e), (g), and the lower brace in (c). Note that, for example (d) and the upper brace in example (e), the relevant gap is not to the adjacent brace, but to the brace in which its load is reacted; a weighted gap (or interpolated $\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{u}} / \mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{q}}$ ) would be used for the lower brace in (e). Members whose punching load component is reacted by beam shear in the chord member(s) are treated as T&Y-connections, as in example, (b), which looks like a K-connection until we examine the loads. Note that for the upper brace in example (c), its load is reacted partly as in a K-connection and partly by chord shear, so that interpolated values of $\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{u}} / \mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{q}}$ are used. Finally, braces whose load is reacted neither as in K-connections nor by chord shear, are treated as cross connections; in addition to example (f), this becomes the default classification. Some other schemes use T/Y classifications as the default.

The foregoing schemes do not deal with multiplanar connections, even though offshore jackets are really space frames, not planar trusses. Furthermore, these schemes fail to recognize that several braces may contribute simultaneously to the ovalizing load on a joint can, as in launch trusses and the examples shown in Figure Comm. E.3-1. Such load cases may produce a more adverse situation than is recognized by considering the members singly as cross connection braces.

An alternative approach addresses these shortcomings through the use of a computed ovalizing parameter, $\alpha$ , as defined in Figure Comm. E.3-2. This is the same $\alpha$ as used in Table Comm. F.1-1 for fatigue SCF. $\alpha$ is computed in turn for each brace end (the reference brace being examined), for each load case of interest.

Connections with $\alpha$ close to unity would be designed as gap K-connections, provided the corresponding brace pairs can be identified. The dominant brace end in a connection with $\alpha$ close to 1.7 would be designed as a T- or Y-connection. Connections with $\alpha$ close to 2.4 would be designed as cross connections. Connections with intermediate values of $\alpha$ , between K and T/Y or between T/Y and cross, would be designed with interpolated values of $Q_{u} / Q_{q}$ with the interpolation based on the $\alpha$ value. In cases where $\alpha$ exceeds 2.4, or where a low value of $\alpha$ results from multiplanar interaction rather than classical K-joint action, alternative design methods should be investigated, e.g., elasto-plastic finite element analysis or the general collapse analysis of Section E.3.4 herein. The $\alpha$ -based strength criteria of ANSI/AWS D1.1-92, Section 10.5.1 may also be considered; however, caution is advised for $\alpha > 5.5$ or $\beta > 0.9$ . These methods, and their background, are further described in Reference E13.

Load Transfer Across Chords. One change introduced in the 20th Edition of RP2A affected the capacity of cross joints with a thickened chord can. Prior to this, the simple joint axial capacity was assumed valid if the length of the thickened region was at least that indicated in Figure E.3-3. However, finite element work in Europe clearly showed the RP2A capacity equation could be significantly unconservative (Reference E12). The derating equation then available in Section 10.5.1.2 of ANSI/AWS D1.1-92 was appropriate provided the brace-chord diameter ratio was less than 1.0 (References E12 and E13). Hence, that equation was introduced as Equation E.3.4-1a.

The derating of moment capacity has not been as thoroughly studied as has derating of a axial capacity. It is believed to be less severe and of less consequence. Thus no derating for moment is recommended.

Other Joints. Many platform joints can not be considered simple ones. Design of complex joints as simple joints is often, but not always, conservative. As of early 1983, there were several worldwide experimental programs on stiffened and grouted joints. Work on overlapping joints was also contemplated. The RP2A wording is intended to permit use of these and similar experimental results, even before detailed design guidelines are established.

COMMENTARY F FATIGUE

COMM.F.0 FATIGUE

Introduction. Fatigue has long been recognized as an important consideration for designing offshore structures, and intensive cooperative industry research on tubular joints occupied the full decade of the 1960s. The first Edition of RP2A gave some general statements regarding fatigue and brittle fracture.

More specific criteria were adopted in 1971 and appeared in the 3rd Edition. These criteria included static strength requirements stated in terms of punching shear, along with general guidelines regarding fatigue. These guidelines included a $138\mathrm{MPa}$ (20 ksi) limitation on cyclic nominal stress, coupled with recommendations that simple joints be designed to meet the punching shear criteria and that complex joints be detailed with smooth flowing lines. For typical Gulf of Mexico structures utilizing joint can steels with improved notch toughness, this simple approach sufficed to relegate fatigue and brittle fracture to the status of secondary considerations. However, it was recognized that using higher design stresses (corresponding to steels with over 345 MPa (50 ksi) yield) or more severe loading experience (e.g., dynamic amplification or North Atlantic type wave climate) would require specific reexamination of the fatigue problem.

Concurrently, the AWS Structural Welding Code (Reference F1) adopted similar punching shear requirements, along with a family of S-N curves applicable to tubular joints. The research basis for these code criteria was reviewed in Reference F2. The AWS fatigue criteria were subsequently incorporated by reference into RP2A.

During 1974-77 two successive task groups attempted to define detailed procedures for analysis of cumulative fatigue damage, particularly for structures falling outside the normal Gulf of Mexico experience. Their deliberations revealed a wide diversity of approaches regarding description of wave climate, structural frame analysis, stress concentration factors, fatigue curves, cycle counting methods, and choice of safety factors. Considerable effort had been expended on each of these approaches in terms of data gathering, computer programming, and calibration. Since each approach had its advocates, no consensus on a single method could be reached. Thus, what emerged in the 8th Edition was a qualitative discussion of the elements of detailed fatigue analysis, written to accommodate a number of valid approaches.

In 1977, the static strength requirements were updated to permit substantial reductions in thickness for certain classes of tubular joints (e.g., K-joints with combined axial load and bending). Subsequent design experience has indicated that these new guidelines upset the parity between static strength and fatigue life for Gulf of Mexico structures, which had existed with the previous

rules. As a result, the 11th Edition expanded the allowable cyclic stress guidelines to assure ample fatigue lives as part of the normal design process for the large class of structures that do not warrant detailed fatigue analyses.

Recent years have seen a resurgence of research interest in tubular joints and fatigue, particularly on the part of governments bordering the North Sea. These large scale efforts have significantly increased the amount of available data and are prompting a reexamination of fatigue criteria. In particular, the endurance limits in the original AWS criteria have been questioned in light of sea water environments, random loading, and fracture mechanics crack growth considerations. A number of designers and agencies have been using modified criteria which defer or eliminate the fatigue endurance limit. These were reflected in the 11th Edition when API included S-N curves for tubular joints.

In addition, recent large scale test results emphasized the importance of weld profile control. A lower set of S-N curves was included to bracket the range of fatigue performance that can result from typical variations in fabrication practice. Changes to the static strength requirements for tubular joints were adopted in 1982 and appeared in Supplement 1 to the 13th Edition. Subsequently in 1983, the changes were expanded and included in the 15th Edition. In that same year, a work group was formed to review the previously adopted allowable cyclic stress guidelines with respect to revised static strength requirements and to redefine detailed procedures for analysis of cumulative fatigue damage.

In 1986, an improved simplified fatigue analysis approach replacing the allowable cyclic stress guidelines was adopted in the 17th Edition along with changes to the provisions for detailed fatigue analysis reflecting greater consensus regarding preferred methods of analysis, description of seastates, structural frame analysis, S-N curves, and stress concentration factors.

New Gulf of Mexico guideline wave heights were adopted in the 20th Edition of the RP2A. Therefore, the simplified fatigue analysis provisions were recalibrated in 1992. In addition to adjusting the Allowable Peak Hot Spot Stress values for the simplified fatigue analysis provisions, the 20th Edition includes changes to the detailed fatigue analysis provisions to the effect that only the spectral analysis techniques should be used for determining stress response.

For both the fatigue design and analysis procedures, use of unfactored （$\gamma = 1.0)$ loads is recommended. Since it is primarily the environmental loading which produces stress reversals, there does not appear to be any advantage to an LRFD format. The fatigue design procedure applies a uniform fatigue damage criterion which has been shown to give results similar to a uni

form reliability approach. The API PRAC-15 fatigue reliability study (Reference F25) compared results of a uniform safety index criterion, with the best available estimates of the random variable parameters, to those from a uniform fatigue damage criterion. The allowable stresses derived from the two criteria varied only slightly.

Fatigue Related Definitions. Some terms, when applied to fatigue, have specific meanings. Several such terms are defined below:

1. Hot Spot Stress: The hot spot stress is the stress in the immediate vicinity of a structural discontinuity.   
2. Mean Zero-Crossing Period: The mean zero-crossing period is the average time between successive crossings with a positive slope (up crossings) of the zero axis in a time history.   
3. Nominal Stress: The nominal stress is the stress determined from member section properties and the resultant forces and moments at the member end. The section properties must account for the existence of thickened or flared stub ends.   
4. Random Waves: Random waves represent the irregular surface elevations and associated water particle kinematics of the marine environment. Random waves can be represented analytically by a summation of sinusoidal waves of different heights, periods, phases, and directions.   
5. Regular Waves: Regular waves are unidirectional waves having cyclical water particle kinematics and surface elevation.   
6. S-N Curve: S-N curves represent empirically determined relationships between stress range and number of cycles to failure.   
7. Seastate: An oceanographic wave condition which for a specified period of time can be characterized as a stationary random process.   
8. Significant Wave Height: The significant wave height is the average height of the highest 1/3 of all the individual waves present in a seastate.   
9. Steady State: Steady state refers to the response of a structure to waves when the transient effects caused by the assumed initial conditions have become insignificant due to damping.   
10. Stress Concentration Factor: The stress concentration factor for a particular stress component and location on a tubular connection is the ratio of the hot spot stress to the nominal stress at the cross section containing the hot spot.   
11. Transfer Function: A transfer function defines the ratio of a structural response quantity to the wave height as a function of frequency.

COMM.F.1 FATIGUE DESIGN

For typical shallow water structures in familiar wave climates, allowable peak stresses based on prior detailed fatigue analyses can be used for fatigue design. For typical Gulf of Mexico template structures with natural periods less than three seconds and under $122\mathrm{m}$ (400 ft) water depth, allowable hot spot stresses have been derived based on calibration with detailed fatigue analyses. The simplified fatigue analysis approach using these allowable stresses and the basis for the stresses are described below. This procedure replaces the method contained in the 16th Edition of RP2A, which was based on an allowable peak hot spot stress of 414 MPa (60 ksi) due to an $18\mathrm{m}$ (60 ft) wave plus associated wind and current. In the former procedure specific assumed stress concentration factors were applied to derive allowable brace end punching shear stresses.

Simplified Fatigue Assessment. The following simplified fatigue analysis provisions may be applied to tubular joints in template type platforms in less than $122\mathrm{m}$ (400 ft) of water constructed of ductile steels, with redundant structural framing and with natural periods less than three seconds. The specific analysis procedure described below is calibrated for a typical Gulf of Mexico wave climate but can be modified for application to different design conditions. The simplified fatigue analysis involves designing all tubular joints in the structure such that the peak hot spot stresses for the fatigue design wave do not exceed the allowable peak hot spot stresses.

(a) Fatigue Design Wave. The fatigue design wave is the reference level wave for the platform water depth as defined in Figure C.3.7-3. This wave should be applied to the structure without wind, current, and gravity load effects using a load factor of 1.0. Tide as defined in Figure C.3.7-7 should be included. The wave force calculations per Section C.3.3 should be followed except that the omnidirectional wave should be applied in all design directions with wave kinematics factor equal to 0.88.   
(b) Allowable Peak Hot Spot Stresses. The allowable peak hot spot stress, $S_{\mathbf{p}}$ , is determined from Figure Comm. F.1-1 or Comm. F.1-2 as a function of water depth, member location, S-N curve and design fatigue life. The design fatigue life should be at least twice the service life. Members framed above the waterline and members extending down to and included in the framing level immediately below the fatigue design wave trough elevation are considered waterline members. The S-N Curve to be used depends upon the weld profile as described in Section F.4.   
(c) Peak Hot Spot Stress for the Fatigue Design Wave. The peak hot spot stress at a joint should be taken as the maximum value of the following expression calculated at both the chord and brace sides of the tubular joint.

$$\left| \operatorname{S C F}_{\mathbf{a x}} f_{\mathbf{a x}} \right| + \sqrt{\left(\operatorname{S C F}_{\mathrm{i p b}} f_{\mathrm{i p b}}\right)^{2} + \left(\operatorname{S C F}_{\mathrm{o p b}} f_{\mathrm{o p b}}\right)^{2}}$$

(Comm.F.1-1)

where $f_{\mathrm{ax}}$ , $f_{\mathrm{ipb}}$ and $f_{\mathrm{opb}}$ are the nominal member end axial, in-plane bending and out-of-plane bending stresses, and $\mathrm{SCF}_{\mathrm{ax}}$ , $\mathrm{SCF}_{\mathrm{ipb}}$ and $\mathrm{SCF}_{\mathrm{opb}}$ are the corresponding stress concentration factors for axial, in-plane bending, and out-of-plane bending stresses for the chord or the brace side. Stress concentration factors are discussed in Section Comm. F.5. Several sets of empirical formulas for estimating SCF's are referenced in Comm. F.5. In addition, Table Comm. F.1-1 includes SCF's developed from one of the referenced examples that may be used with Equation Comm. F.1-1 for simple joints classified and designed per Section E.3.1. SCFs developed from other references may be larger for some joint parameters. In general, four wave approach directions (end-on, broadside, and two diagonal) and sufficient wave positions relative to the platform should be considered to identify the peak hot spot stress at each member end for the fatigue design wave.

Comm. F.1.1 Derivation of Allowable Peak Hot Spot Stress. The allowable peak hot spot stress given in Figures Comm. F.1-1 and Comm. F.1-2 is derived as a function of the parameter, $\mathbf{g}$ , which defines how a structure responds to different wave heights. This procedure is documented in more detail in References F28 and F29. There are three basic assumptions to this approach:

1. The stress range, S, is related to the wave height, H, in the form

$\mathbf{S} = \mathbf{C}\mathbf{H}\pmb{\varepsilon}$ (Comm.F.1-2)

where $\mathbf{C}$ is a calibrated constant and $\mathbf{g}$ is a calibrated exponent.

2. The S-N Curve can be written

$$\mathbf{N S}^{\mathrm{m}} = \mathbf{K}. \tag{Comm. F.1-3}$$

where $\mathbf{K}$ is constant and $\mathbf{N}$ and $\mathbf{m}$ are defined in Figure F.4-1.

3. The long-term wave height distribution can be represented by the sum of two Weibull distributions as shown in Figure Comm. F.1-3 for normal and hurricane conditions.

Based on the above three assumptions, a closed form expression for the fatigue damage can be written:

$$\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{s}} = \frac{\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{s}}}{\mathrm{K}} \mathrm{C}^{\mathrm{m}} \left(\mathrm{Y}_{0} + \mathrm{Y}_{1}\right) \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \tag{Comm. F.1-4}$$

where $\mathbf{D}_{\mathbf{s}}$ is the fatigue damage accumulated over the service life and $\mathbf{T}_{\mathbf{s}}$ is the service life of the structure,

| CHORDSCF | K | 1.0 | αA | 2/3 A | 3/2 A |
| CHORDSCF | T&Y | 1.7 | αA | 2/3 A | 3/2 A |

Where $\mathbf{A} = 1.8\sqrt{\gamma}\tau$ sin $\theta$ and all other terms are defined in Figure E.3-1.

$$\begin{array}{l} \mathbf{Y}_{\mathbf{o}} = \frac{\mathbf{N}_{\mathbf{o}}}{\mathbf{T}} \mathbf{H}_{\mathbf{o}}^{\mathbf{g m}} (\ln \mathbf{N}_{\mathbf{o}})^{- \mathbf{g m} / \xi_{0}} \Gamma (1 + \frac{\mathbf{g m}}{\xi_{0}}) \\ \ldotp \ldotp \ldotp \ldotp \ldotp \ldotp \ldotp \ldotp \ldotp \ldotp \ldotp \ldotp \ldotp \ldotp \ldotp \ldotp \ldotp \ldotp \ldotp \ldotp \ldotp \ldotp \ldotp \ldotp \ldotp \ldotp \ldotp \ldotp \ldotp \ldotp \ldotp \ldotp \ldotp \ldotp \dots . \\ \end{array}$$

$$\begin{array}{l} \mathrm{Y}_{1} = \frac{\mathrm{N}_{1}}{\mathrm{T}} \mathrm{H f}^{\mathrm{g m}} (\ln \mathrm{N}_{1})^{- \mathrm{g m} / \xi_{1}} \Gamma (1 + \frac{\mathrm{g m}}{\xi_{1}}) \\ \ldotp \dots \tag{Comm. F. 1-4b} \\ \end{array}$$

where $\Gamma (\cdot)$ is the gamma function and $\mathbf{N}_0,\mathbf{N}_1,\mathbf{H}_0,\mathbf{H}_1,\xi_0,\xi_1$ , and T define the wave climate as shown in Figure Comm. F.1-3.

The hot spot stress range, $\mathbf{S}_f$ , corresponding to the fatigue design wave height, $\mathbf{H}_f$ , can be written as follows:

$$\mathbf{S}_{f} = \mathrm{C H}_{f}^{f} \quad \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \tag{Comm.F.1-5}$$

By substituting C from Equation Comm. F.1-4 into Equation Comm. F.1-5, substituting the calculated fatigue life $\mathbf{T}_{\mathbf{f}} = \mathbf{T}_{\mathbf{s}} / \mathbf{D}_{\mathbf{s}}$ and simplifying, the hot spot stress range can be written:

$$\mathbf{S}_{f} = \left[ \frac{\mathbf{K} \mathbf{H} f^{\mathrm{g m}}}{\mathbf{T}_{f} \left(\mathbf{Y}_{0} + \mathbf{Y}_{1}\right)} \right]^{1 / \mathrm{m}} \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \tag{Comm.F.1-6}$$

It is observed that $\mathbf{T_f}$ represents the calculated fatigue life. If this value is replaced by the design fatigue life, $\mathbf{T_d}$ , then Equation Comm. F.1-6 gives the allowable hot spot stress range corresponding to $\mathbf{H_f}$ , i.e.,

$$\mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{r}} = \left[ \frac{\mathrm{K H}_{l}^{\mathrm{g m}}}{\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{d}} \left(\mathrm{Y}_{0} + \mathrm{Y}_{1}\right)} \right]^{1 / \mathrm{m}} \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \tag{Comm. F.1-7}$$

where $\mathbf{T_d} = \mathbf{T_s}$ (S.F.) per Section F.2.5.

![](API_RP_2A-LRFD_1st/chunk2_63f57d034739bbe8b143cf84e2197c0d23612578764617ffc9fc7ea7b285052f.jpg)

In order to calculate the allowable peak hot spot stress, $S_{p}$ , in Figures Comm. F.1-1 and Comm. F.1-2 from the allowable hot spot stress range, $S_{r}$ , in Equation Comm. F.1-7, the stress cycle ratio $R$ must be known. This ratio is defined as:

$$R = S_{\min } / S_{\max } \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \tag{Comm.F.1-8}$$

The $\mathbf{S_p}$ values in the figures are then calculated from

$$\mathbf{S}_{\mathrm{p}} = \mathbf{S}_{\mathrm{r}} / (1 - \mathrm{R}) \quad \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \tag{Comm.F.1-9}$$

The allowable stress curves in Comm. F.1 were generated based on Equations Comm. F.1-7 and Comm. F.1-9. The necessary parameters to be input are the S-N Curve constants, the design fatigue life $\mathbf{T}_{\mathrm{d}}$ , the long-term wave height distribution parameters, the fatigue design wave height $\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{f}}$ , the stress cycle ratio $\mathbf{R}$ , and the parameter $\mathbf{g}$ .

Figure Comm. F.1-1 is based on the S-N Curve X parameters （$\mathbf{m} = 4.38$ and $\mathbf{K} = 2.44\times 10^{11})$ $\mathbf{T}_{\mathrm{d}}$ of 40 or 100 years, $\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{f}}$ per Figure C.3.7-3, and a 100-year wave height distribution defined by the following parameters:

$$\begin{array}{l} \mathbf{N}_{0} = 1 \times 10^{9}, \\ \mathrm{H}_{0} = 12. 2 \mathrm{m} (40 \mathrm{f t .}) \\ \begin{array}{r l} \xi_{0} & = 1. 0, \end{array} \\ \mathbf{N}_{1} = 1 \times 10^{6}, \\ \mathrm{H}_{1} = 22. 9 \mathrm{m} (75 \mathrm{f t .}) \\ \begin{array}{r l} \xi_{1} & = 1. 0. \end{array} \\ \end{array}$$

Figure Comm. F.1-2 is based on the same parameters except for the $\mathbf{X}^{\prime}$ S-N Curve values of $\mathbf{m} = 3.74$ and $\mathbf{K} = 1.79\times 10^{10}$ . Values to be used for $\mathbf{g}$ and $\mathbf{R}$ were identified through a calibration exercise described below. Variables considered in calibrating $\mathbf{g}$ were the platform natural period, waterline geometry, and the location of the joint in the structure. The recommended values of $\mathbf{g}$ are not shown in Figures Comm. F.1-1 and Comm. F.1-2; instead, the allowable $\mathbf{S_p}$ has been derived directly. Long-term wave height distribution for water depths less than $15\mathrm{m}$ (50 ft.) cannot be easily generalized. The distributions used are described in more detail in Reference F29. Allowable $\mathbf{S_p}$ values for this water depth range may be adjusted based on the site-specific wave height distribution data.

Comm. F.1.2 Calibration of $\mathbf{g}$ (based on a typical Gulf of Mexico wave climate). From the approach outlined above, there are three basic variables, any one of which can be calculated given the other two. These are the fatigue life $\mathbf{T}_f$ , the hot spot stress range $\mathbf{S}_f$ from the fatigue design wave, and the parameter $\mathbf{g}$ . In order to calibrate values of $\mathbf{g}$ to the results of a detailed fatigue analysis, only the values $\mathbf{S}_f$ and $\mathbf{T}_f$ need to be calculated. The wave height distribution parameters $\mathbf{N}_0$ , $\mathbf{H}_0$ , $\xi_0$ , $\mathbf{N}_1$ , $\mathbf{H}_1$ , $\xi_1$ , and $\mathbf{T}$ must be derived from the long-term wave climate used to calculate $\mathbf{T}_f$ . In order to simplify

![](API_RP_2A-LRFD_1st/chunk2_e1369a575a20e9926e4d990d18ed3e531914dee7d6117a3eb4a4c2000d71959d.jpg)

Where: $\mathbf{H}_0$ is the maximum normal wave height over period T.   
$\mathbf{H}_{1}$ is the maximum hurricane wave height over period $\mathbf{T}$ .   
$\mathbf{N}_0$ is the number of wave cycles from normal distribution over period $\mathbf{T}$ .   
$\mathbf{N}_{1}$ is the number of wave cycles from hurricane distribution over period $\mathbf{T}$ .   
T is the duration of the long-term wave height distribution.   
$\xi_0$ is the parameter defining the shape of the Weibull normal distribution. Value of 1.0 corresponding to the exponential distribution results in a straight line.   
$\xi_{1}$ is the parameter defining the shape of the Weibull hurricane distribution.

the fatigue design procedures, hot spot stress ranges were calculated from peak hot spot stresses from the fatigue design wave using the total base shear cycle ratio R. Typical values of R ranged from -0.15 to -0.50 and are dependent on water depth.

Detailed fatigue calculations were performed on four platforms. These platforms ranged in water depth from 17.5 to $95.7\mathrm{m}$ (58 to 314 ft.) and in natural period up to 2.85 sec. The following observations were noted for the calibrated $\mathbf{g}$ values.

1. The allowable peak hot spot stress values given in Figures Comm. F.1-1 and Comm. F.1-2 are based on blanket $\mathbf{g}$ values of 1.2 for waterline members and 1.3 for other members. These $\mathbf{g}$ values represent approximate lower bounds to the calibrated data.   
2. The greatest scatter in the $\mathbf{g}$ values occurs consistently in the framing level above still water, which, in part, can be attributed to the inundation effects.   
3. The least scatter in the $\mathbf{g}$ values was observed in the vertical diagonal members and mudline framing members, where the member end stresses are governed by the frame action response to wave loading. These $\mathbf{g}$ values tended to be consistently greater than the lower bound values selected.   
4. The blanket $\mathbf{g}$ values account for the effects of dynamics for structures with natural periods less than three seconds. However, the $\mathbf{g}$ values and consequently the allowable hot spot stresses decrease as natural period increases, particularly for vertical diagonals and mudline members.

Comm. F.1.3 Selected SCF Formulas. The stress concentration factors given in Table Comm. F.1-1 for the chord are based upon the modified formulas (References F7 and F20) for K, T, and X joints. The brace side SCF formula is that suggested by Marshall (Reference F7) with a reduction factor of 0.625. In these equations, a computed alpha value as proposed in Reference F20 can be substituted for $\alpha$ where multi-planar effects are important.

COMM.F.2 FATIGUE ANALYSIS

A simplified fatigue analysis may be used as a first step for structures in deep water or frontier areas. However, a detailed analysis of cumulative fatigue damage should always be performed. A detailed analysis is necessary to design fatigue sensitive locations which may not follow the assumptions inherent in the simplified analysis.

Comm. F.2.1 Wave Climate. Wave climate information is required for any fatigue analysis, and obtaining it often requires a major effort with significant lead time. Wave climates may be derived from both recorded data and hindcasts. Sufficient data should exist to characterize the long term oceanographic conditions at the platform site. Several formats are permissible and the choice depends on compatibility with the analytical

procedures being used. However, for each format the wave climate is defined by a series of seastates, each characterized by its wave energy spectrum and physical parameters together with a probability of occurrence (percent of time). Formats that may be used include the following:

(1) Two parameter scatter diagrams. These describe the joint probability of various combinations of significant wave height and mean zero-crossing period. Typically, 60 to 150 seastates are used to describe most sea environments. While a reduced number may be used for analysis, a sufficient number of seastates should be used to adequately define the scatter diagram and develop full structural response. If the scatter diagram is condensed the effect of dynamic excitation, interaction between wave length and platform geometry, and drag force nonlinearity should be considered. When condensing seastates of different height or period the resulting seastates should yield equivalent or greater damage than the original seastates. This format does not give any information on wave directionality.   
(2) Directional scatter diagrams. Each seastate is characterized by three parameters: significant wave height, mean zero-crossing period and central direction of wave approach (Reference F3). If the measured data do not include wave directionality, directions may be estimated on the basis of wind measurements, local topography, and hindcasting, provided sufficient care is exercised.   
(3) Directional scatter diagrams with spreading. Each seastate is characterized by four parameters: significant wave height, mean zero-crossing period, central direction of wave approach, and directional spreading. The directional spreading function, $\mathbf{D}(\theta)$ , defines the distribution of wave energy in a seastate with direction and must satisfy:

$$\begin{array}{l} \pi / 2 \\ \int_{- \pi / 2}^{\pi / 2} \mathrm{D} (\theta) \mathrm{d} \theta = 1 \end{array} \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \tag{Comm.F.2-1}$$

where $\theta$ is measured from the central direction. A commonly used spreading function (Reference F7) is:

$$\mathbf{D} (\theta) = \mathbf{C}_{\mathrm{n}} \cos^{\mathrm{n}} \theta \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \tag{Comm.F.2-2}$$

where $n$ is a positive integer (number) and $C_n$ is a coefficient selected such that Equation Comm. F.2-1 is satisfied. A value of $n$ equal to zero corresponds to the case when the energy is equally distributed in all directions. Observations of wind driven seas show that an appropriate spreading function is a cosine squared function （$n = 2)$ . For situations where limited fetch restricts degree of spread a value of $n = 4$ has been found to be appropriate. Other methods for directional spreading are given in Reference F21.

(4) Bimodal spectra. Up to eight parameters are used to combine swell with locally generated waves. Typically, swell is more undirectional than wind generated waves and thus spreading should not be considered unless measured data shows otherwise (Reference F22).

Data gathered in more complete formats can always be reduced to the simpler ones. For recorded data and hindcasting, spectral characterizations described by Borgman and Cardone (References F4 and F5) may serve as starting points.

Comm. F.2.2 Structural Modeling and Analysis. The space frame model for fatigue analysis should include all important characteristics of the stiffness, mass, energy dissipation and loading properties of the structure and foundation components of the platform. The analytical model consists primarily of beam elements. The adequacy of calculated member end stresses for fatigue analysis is contingent on the modeling techniques used. The model used for strength analysis may require refinements such as the addition or modification of members which are fatigue sensitive. Asymmetry in platform stiffness or mass distribution may lead to significant torsional response which should be considered.

Stiffness: The model should include the three dimensional distribution of platform stiffness. The member intersections should be modeled such that the resulting nominal member end stresses are consistent with their subsequent use in fatigue analysis. For typical jacket members, nominal brace stresses should be computed at the intersections of the brace and chord centerlines. For large diameter chords or short braces, local joint stiffness should be considered. One modeling technique which has been used to represent the joint stiffness is to simulate chord stiffness between the intersection of the centerlines and the chord face as a rigid link with springs at the face representing the chord shell flexibility, and hence member end stresses should be calculated at the face of the chord. Rigid links should not be used without also considering chord shell flexibility.

The stiffness of appurtenances such as launch cradles, mudmats, J-tubes, risers, skirt pile guides, etc., should be included in the model if they contribute significantly to the overall global stiffness of the structure. The stiffness of the conductors and horizontal framing levels should be included. In addition, down to and including the level immediately below the design wave trough elevation, sufficient detail should be included to perform a fatigue analysis of the individual components of the framing. Similar detailing of the mudline level is required if the conductors are considered in the foundation. Consideration of structural components such as mudmats, shear connectors, conductor guides, etc., may require finite element types other than beam elements (e.g., shell, plate, solid). The stiffness of the deck should be considered in sufficient detail to adequately represent the deck-jacket interface.

A linear representation of the foundation may be used provided the stiffness coefficients reflect the cyclic response for those seastates contributing significantly to fatigue damage.

Mass: The mass model should include structural steel, equipment, conductors, appurtenances, grout, marine growth, entrapped water, and added mass. A lumped mass model is sufficient to obtain global structure response. However, this method may not adequately predict local dynamic response. Where necessary, local responses should be examined. The equipment mass included in the model should consider all equipment supported by the structure during any given operation on the platform. If the equipment mass is predicted to vary significantly for different operations during the platform life, it is appropriate to perform independent analyses and combine fatigue damage. The added mass may be estimated as the mass of the displaced water for motion transverse to the longitudinal axis of the individual structural framing and appurtenances.

Energy Dissipation: The choice of damping factors can have a profound effect, and values of $2\%$ critical and less have been suggested on the basis of measurements in low seastates. Including structural velocities in the calculation of drag forces increases the total system damping. For noncompliant structures, this increase in damping is not observed in measurements and consequently should not be considered. For compliant structures such as guyed towers, these effects may be considered in addition to a $2\%$ structural (including foundation) damping.

Natural Period: For structural periods above three seconds, dynamic amplification is important, particularly for the lower seastates which may contribute the most to long term fatigue damage. Several authors have shown the desirability of retaining the detailed information available from a full static analysis and adding the inertial forces due to dynamic amplification of the first few modes (mode acceleration or static back-substitution method, Reference F24). A pure modal analysis using a limited number of modes misses the essentially static response of some modes.

Since the natural period of a platform can vary considerably depending upon design assumptions and operational deck mass, a theoretical period should be viewed critically if it falls in a valley in the platform base shear transfer function. The period should be shifted by as much as 5 to $10\%$ to a more conservative location with respect to the transfer function. This should be accomplished by adjusting mass or stiffness within reasonable limits. The choice of which parameter to modify is platform specific and depends upon deck mass, soil conditions and structural configuration. It should be recognized that adjusting the foundation stiffness will alter the member loads in the base of the structure which can be fatigue sensitive.

Loading: The applied cyclic loads should be represented such that the effect of load distribution along the

member is included in the member end stresses. Distributed loads on brace members need to be considered only between intersection points. Loads attributed to conductors and appurtenances such as launch cradles, mudmat framing, J-tubes, risers, skirt pile guides, anodes, etc., should be considered. The choice of wave theory, as well as drag and mass coefficients, should be examined as they may differ from those used in strength analyses of design wave loads. Attention should be given to modeling of conductor guide framing to ensure correct vertical wave loads. When the loading varies significantly for different operations during the platform life (e.g., towing, drilling and production), it is appropriate to perform independent analyses and combine the fatigue damage.

Tides, currents and marine growth each affect fatigue. For everyday waves, tides will have little effect. However, the tide and surge associated with storm seas can have a significant effect. For example, they may cause the wave crest to inundate a member or entire jacket level, which would otherwise be dry. Such effects should be considered.

Current is a complicated phenomenon that is difficult to account for in a fatigue analysis. Since fatigue considers the stress range, the static effect of current can be neglected. For large waves or currents, the drag will increase the crest-to-trough wave force difference and affect platform dynamics. While these effects can be important, analysis technology is lacking.

Marine growth has a detrimental effect on fatigue life of members subjected to local wave loading, and in general it has a similar effect on members controlled by global deformations. A marine growth profile should be specified for the maximum thickness and roughness expected or allowed at the platform site, if it produces conservative results. A simplified analysis is useful in studying the effect of marine growth on global response. Marine growth affects platform added mass, member drag diameter, and drag coefficient.

At present an environmental load factor $\gamma_{\mathrm{w}}$ of 1.0 is recommended for the detailed fatigue analysis. Uncertainties in the loading can be accounted for in the safety factor on fatigue life described in Section F.2.5.

Comm. F.2.2.1 Spectral Fatigue Analysis. Several approaches are available for determining stress response to seastate loadings. In general, a spectral analysis should be used to properly account for the actual distribution of wave energy over the entire frequency range. The spectral approach can be subdivided based upon the method used to develop the transfer function.

(1) Transfer functions developed using regular waves in the time domain.

- Characterize the wave climate using either the two, three, four or eight parameter format (as described in Comm. F.2.1).

- Select a sufficient number of frequencies to define all the peaks and valleys inherent in the jacket response transfer function. A typical set of frequencies is illustrated in Figure Comm. F.2-1. A simplified analysis (Reference F7) that develops a global base shear transfer function may be helpful in defining frequencies to be used in the detailed analysis.

- Select a wave height corresponding to each frequency. A constant wave steepness that is appropriate for the wave climate can be used. For the Gulf of Mexico, a steepness between 1:20 and 1:25 is generally used. A minimum height of one foot and a maximum height equal to the extreme design wave height should be used.

- Compute a stress range transfer function at each point where fatigue damage is to be accumulated for a minimum of four platform directions (end-on, broadside and two diagonal). For jackets with unusual geometry or where wave directionality, spreading or current is considered, more directions may be required. At each frequency, a point on the transfer function is determined by passing an Airy wave of the appropriate height through the structure and dividing the response stress range by the wave height. The analysis procedure must eliminate transient effects by achieving steady state conditions. A sufficient number of time steps in the wave cycle at which member stresses are computed should be selected to determine the maximum brace hot spot stress range. A minimum of four hot spot locations at both the brace and chord side of the connection should be considered.

- Compute the stress response spectra. In a spectral fatigue analysis in its most general form, each seastate is represented by a power spectral density function $\mathbf{S}_{\alpha}(\omega)$ for each direction of wave approach $\alpha$ , where $\omega$ is circular frequency. At each location of interest, the platform stress response spectrum for each seastate is:

$$\begin{array}{r l} \mathbf{S}_{\alpha , \alpha} (\omega) & = \int | \mathbf{H} (\omega , \theta) |^{2} \mathbf{D} (\theta) \mathbf{S}_{\alpha} (\omega) d \theta . \dots . (C o m m. F. 2 - 3) \\ & - \pi / 2 \end{array}$$

where: $\theta$ is measured from the central wave approach direction, $\mathbf{H}(\omega ,\theta)$ is the transfer function and $\mathbf{D}(\theta)$ is the spreading function as defined in Comm. F.2.1(3).

Several approximations and linearizations are introduced into the fatigue analysis with this approach:

- The way in which waves of different frequencies in a seastate are coupled by the nonlinear drag force is ignored.   
Assuming a constant wave steepness has the effect of linearizing the drag force about the height selected for each frequency. Consequently, drag forces due to waves at that frequency with large

heights will be underpredicted, while drag forces due to waves with smaller heights will be over-predicted.

(2) Transfer functions developed using regular waves in the frequency domain. This approach is similar to method (1) except that the analysis is linearized prior to the calculation of structural response. In linearizing the applied wave force, drag forces are approximated by sinusoidally varying forces and inundation effects are approximated or ignored. As a result, the equations of motion can then be solved without performing direct time integration. For typical small waves the effects of linearization are not of great importance; however, for large waves they may be significant if inundation effects are ignored.

(3) Transfer functions developed using random waves in the time domain (Reference F23). The following steps are taken in this approach:

- Characterize the wave climate in terms of sea-state scatter diagrams.

-- Simulate random wave time histories of finite length for a few selected reference seastates.

- Compute response stress time histories at each point of a structure where fatigue life is to be determined and transform the response stress time histories into response stress spectra.

- Generate "exact" transfer functions from wave and response stress spectra.

- Calculate pseudo transfer functions for all the remaining seastates considered using the few "exact" transfer functions.

- Calculate pseudo response stress spectra as described in method (1).

This method can take into account nonlinearities arising from wave-structure interaction and avoids difficulties in selecting wave heights and frequencies for transfer function generation.

Comm. F.2.3 Local Stresses. In evaluating local scale stress at hot spot locations the stress concentration factor used should be consistent with the corresponding S-N curve; see Sections F.4 and F.5.

Comm. F.2.4 Cumulative Damage. Various approaches to a Miner cumulative damage summation have been used. In all cases, the effects of short term seastates are summed to yield the long term damage or predict the fatigue life.

For a spectral analysis, the response stress spectrum may be used to estimate the short-term stress range distribution by assuming either:

(1) a narrow band Rayleigh distribution. For a Rayleigh distribution the short term damage may be calculated in closed form.

(2) a broad band Rice distribution, neglecting the negative peaks.   
(3) time series simulation and cycle counting via rainfall, range pair, or some other algorithm.

Damage due to large waves which have significant drag forces or crest elevations should be computed and included in the total fatigue damage.

Comm. F.2.5 Fatigue Life. A calculated fatigue life should be viewed with skepticism. Where possible, the entire procedure being used should be calibrated against available failure/nonfailure experience. Although $97\%$ of the available data falls on the safe side of the recommended S-N curves, additional uncertainties in the analysis may result in a $95\%$ prediction interval for failures ranging from 0.5 to 20 times the calculated fatigue life at $\mathbf{D}_{\mathbf{r}}$ of unity. Calibration hindcasts falling outside this range should prompt a reexamination of the procedures used.

In light of the uncertainty, the calculated fatigue life should be a multiple of the intended service life. Structural redundancy and the extent of inservice inspections should be considered in selecting the safety factor on fatigue life. Doubling the fatigue life requires about a $10\%$ increase in joint can thickness.

Uncertainties in fatigue life estimates can be logically evaluated in a probabilistic framework. A fatigue reliability model based on the log-normal distribution is presented in Reference F25. This model is compatible with the detailed fatigue analysis methods described above. The sources of uncertainty in fatigue life (which is considered to be a random variable) are described explicitly.

COMM. F.4 S-N CURVES FOR TUBULAR CONNECTIONS

The fundamental criterion for tubular joints, curve X, was derived from hot spot strain range measurements and fatigue tests to failure, placing a wide variety of as-welded configurations on a common basis. Although there has been some variation in technique among various investigators contributing to the data base, typical hot spot strain gages were centered within $6\mathrm{mm}$ ( $\frac{1}{4}$ in) to $0.1\sqrt{\mathrm{Rt}}$ of the weld toes, with a gage length of $3\mathrm{mm}$ ( $\frac{1}{8}$ in) and oriented perpendicular to the weld. Here R and t refer to the outside radius and thickness of the member instrumented, either the chord or brace. Due to the steep stress gradients near intersecting tubes, larger gages further from the weld indicate stresses which are too low.

The microscopic notch or stress singularity at the weld toe is excluded from this definition of hot spot stress, but rather is included in the S-N curve. In turn, the S-N curve should be qualified as to the severity of these notches, which are a function of both weld size and profile quality. Curve X applies where the as-welded profile merges smoothly with the adjoining base metal, as shown in Figure Comm. F.4-1a and described in

L.1.3.4. Where such profile control is not practiced, as in Figure Comm. F4-1b, lower fatigue performance and S-N curve $\mathbf{X}^{\prime}$ apply. Furthermore, when the branch thickness exceeds a certain reference thickness, the corresponding larger weld notches further degrade fatigue performance, even for weld toe hotspots on the chord side. A summary of the relevant API provisions is shown in Figure Comm. F.4-2. These were adapted from ANSI/AWS D1.1-92, for which background and supporting data are given in References F31 to F33.

COMM. F.5 STRESS CONCENTRATION FACTORS

Finite element thin shell analyses may be used to obtain hot spot strains compatible with curve X (or $\mathbf{X}^{\prime}$ ), provided the mesh is fine enough to reproduce the steep stress gradients and results corresponding to the actual weld toe location, rather than the midplane intersection, are used. Isoparametric thick shell and solid elements can be used for even more direct modeling of the weld zone.

Empirical Formulas. Several sets of empirical formulas are available to estimate hot spot SCF; examples are as follows:

1. The Kuang formulas (Reference F30) are derived from correlation with extensive thin shell finite element analyses. When used to hindcast hot spot

strains for fatigue tests in the data base for Curve X, the results are conservative when compared with the original correlation based on measured strains (Reference F6), as shown in Figure Comm. F.5-1. It should be noted that brace side SCF was revised by a reduction factor of 5/8. This factor only applies to the amplified part of the stress as shown in Figure Comm. F.5-1.

$$\mathrm{S C F}_{\text{B R A C E}} = 1 + 5 / 8 \left(\mathrm{S C F}_{\text{K U A N G}} - 1\right).$$

A more general reduction factor derived by Marshall is discussed in Reference F7.

2. SCF formulas based on the Kellogg formula (Reference F7). This set of SCF formulas has provision for grouted joints. However, these formulas should be used with caution since recent data suggest that grout may only effect SCFs for loadings and joint geometries that cause chord ovalization.   
3. SCF formulas developed by Lloyds Register, London (References F14 and F15), that are derived from strain gaged acrylic models. These are based on physically reasonable limits rather than statistical correlation techniques.   
4. Other more recent works by Gibstein (Reference F16), Buitrago (Reference F26), and Tebbett (Reference F27).

Caution should be exercised when using parametric equations out of their ranges of calibration.

Cumulative fatigue damage should be assessed at a minimum of four points around each tubular connection. At saddle points, superimpose axial and out-of-plane bending hot spot stresses, while at crown points, superimpose axial and in-plane bending hot spot stresses as illustrated in Figure Comm. F.5-2(a). The nominal brace member stresses $\mathbf{f_{ax}}$ , $\mathbf{f_{ibp}}$ , $\mathbf{f_{opb}}$ , corresponding to three modes of loading are shown in Figure Comm. F.5-2(b). Under combined loading, maximum hot spot stress may occur at circumferential locations other than saddle or crown positions. When assessing damage at eight or more points, the stress distribution should be considered using model test, finite element analysis or parametric studies (Reference F27). When this information is not available, simplified stress distribution formulas (References F17, F18 and F19) may be used.

All SCF formulas listed in this section should, in the strict sense, be used for simple planar joints. The effects of SCF due to loading of out-of-plane brace members should be considered. Use of SCF formulas which incorporate loading interactions of all the relevant braces has been proposed (Reference F20).

Theoretically, joints should be classified by geometry and loading for each time step considered in the fatigue analysis. Since this approach is prohibitively complex, simplified joint classification schemes are typically used. Joints with stresses induced primarily by frame actions may be classified by the maximum loading case for each wave direction considered. If joint static strength design has been performed for that particular direction, the corresponding storm loading case can be used. When classifying joints in the wave zone, interactions between local wave loading and frame actions need to be considered.

Effect of Sea Water. Corrosion fatigue may severely limit the fatigue performance of welded tubular con

nectons in offshore structures. There have been suggestions that design S-N curves derived from tests in air should be devalued to account for the effects of various sea water environments. Although available data indicate that with proper cathodic protection total fatigue life approaches that measured in air, experience shows that over the life of the structure cathodic protection tends to be intermittent with impressed current systems, allowing at least some corrosion fatigue damage. Fatigue cracks which initiate during one of the lapses could continue to grow at an accelerated rate.

Sea water test data available in 1973 (Reference F8) are shown in Figure Comm. F.5-3. Notched and welded specimens, with and without cathodic protection, are plotted along with data from complete tubular connections. The tests which went 109 cycles were welded plate bending specimens; although they did not fail, small growing fatigue cracks were found when the tests were discontinued after about a year of cycling. The trend of the data, together with consideration of the effects of random loading, suggested that the original AWS curve X, which flattens at 2 million cycles, might be unconservative in the higher cycle range. The data as a whole are more consistent with the modified curve X (forerunner of the current API curve X).

The results of more recent tests (References F9 and F13) are shown in Figure Comm. F.5-4. The data are separated two ways:

(1) Butt welds and welds with profile control versus fillet welds and welds without profile control. This distinction is consistent with separate API curves X and $\mathbf{X}^{\prime}$ as described earlier.   
(2) Free corrosion (FC) versus cathodic protection (CP).

Again, the design curves provide a reasonable lower bound to all the data. The free corrosion data tend to crowd a bit closer to the curve than the air data (Figure Comm. F.5-1, and the Gurney scatterband in Figure Comm. F.5-4, but this is accompanied by reduced scatter. Tests with cathodic protection show some tendency toward longer fatigue lives, but there is much more scatter and some early failures at about the same time as for free corrosion. Although fracture mechanics crack growth tests indicate that sea water and cathodic protection should accelerate crack growth rates, the total fatigue life for the as-welded connections tested shows a remarkably consistent lowest-common-denominator, when indexed to the severity of the notch at the toe of the weld.

Research in this area is continuing. However, for the time being, there seems to be no compelling evidence that design S-N curves need to be further devalued, beyond the provisions of Section F.2.5.
